Both behaviors emerge implicitly in pre-trained models, whether the LLM outputs a plan directly or generates a PDDL formulation for a classical solver. Aggressive commitment risks costly failures, while conservative commitment risks excessive LLM calls. This choice pits safety against efficiency, a trade-off that has been neither characterized systematically nor made controllable. We investigate aggressive and conservative LLM planners and formalizers on two partially observable domains, where priors are provided as either explicit statistics or common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs, both strategies reach similar accuracy. Conservative methods achieve fewer failed attempts (safety) at the cost of more API calls (efficiency). Aggressive methods fail more often but replan efficiently only when priors are informative. Interestingly, analysis shows that LLMs treat the provided priors nearly as facts, which risks failure when priors are unreliable. We also explore hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters that adjust the balance between safety and efficiency.

title: Generalized $m$-body mean-field projections for classical simulation of $d$-dimensional Heisenberg-picture dynamics
authors: Federico Tomás B. Pérez, Gabriela Wójtowicz, Matthias Kost, Martin B. Plenio
abstract: Classical simulation of quantum many-body dynamics is challenged by the rapid growth of operator complexity, particularly in higher dimensions where tensor-network methods become increasingly demanding. We develop state-adapted Pauli-weight propagation based on generalized $m$-body mean-field projections, which compress many-body observables into optimal low-body representations in a covariance geometry induced by the initial state. Combined with adaptive Krylov-like restricted Heisenberg dynamics, this provides an alternative to conventional Hilbert--Schmidt Pauli-weight truncation. We derive necessary and conditional sufficient bounds on low-body approximation accuracy using standard operator complexity measures and characterize possible dynamical failure mechanisms of the state-adapted method. Numerical benchmarks demonstrate substantial state-dependent accuracy gains, while identifying regimes of reduced accuracy or violations of Pauli spectral bounds. For a three-dimensional system of $80$ interacting spins, our method achieves strong body-order convergence, close agreement with independently converging tensor-network simulations, and substantially smaller sparse Pauli representations. These results establish state-adapted Pauli propagation as a promising approach to classical simulation of higher-dimensional coherent many-body dynamics.

title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content
authors: Shuanglin Li, Jiaying Lin, Shuquan Ye
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.

title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
authors: Jiachen Yao, Xiyuan Zhang, Annan Yu, Boran Han, Abdul Fatir Ansari, Shuai Zhang, Michael Bohlke-Schneider, Bernie Wang
abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling
authors: Bowei Liu, Xinchen Zhang, Xuhuan Li, Tianlin Zhang, Kaian Jiang, Jingwei Liu, Congyang Zhao, Yifei Qian, Junhong Liu, Zhiheng Li, Yujiu Yang, Yang Cai, Ling Yang
abstract: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.

title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
authors: Bingcong Li, Hao Ma, Michael Muehlebach, Niao He, Yi Ma
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.

title: Projected sensitivity of a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate comagnetometer to proton monopole-dipole interactions
authors: Wenjing Zhou, Diego Blas, Morgan W. Mitchell
abstract: Light spin-zero bosons with scalar and pseudoscalar couplings mediate a parity- and time-reversal-violating monopole-dipole interaction between unpolarized matter and polarized spins. For proton spins, the interaction has been probed directly only at ranges $λ\gtrsim$ 5 mm; below this range, laboratory limits are inferred from neutron-dominated nuclei through nuclear-spin models. We analyze a direct search with a single-domain $^{87}$Rb spinor Bose-Einstein condensate in close proximity to a source mass. The F=1 and F=2 manifolds act as two co-located magnetometers that precess in opposite directions in a magnetic field but in the same direction under the exotic interaction. They thus form a natural comagnetometer, in which the sum of their precession angles suppresses field noise by a measured 44 dB and a weighted sum cancels the field altogether. Taking as a starting point the demonstrated magnetometry [Palacios et al. Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. \textbf{119}, e2115339119 (2022)] and comagnetometry [Gomez et al. Phys. Ref. Lett. \textbf{124}, 170401 (2020)] performance of the $^{87}$Rb single-domain spinor condensate at ICFO [Palacios et al. New J. Phys. \textbf{20}, 053008 (2018)], we study the projected sensitivity as a function of source-mass geometry and in-progress improvements to atom loading methods, trap beam geometry, and magnetic environment. With an insulating bismuth germanate source mass with a spherical top, whose apex sits 50 $μ$m below the center of the condensate, one week of acquisition would reach $|g_s^N g_p^p|\approx 2\times10^{-22}$ with these upgrades and $3\times10^{-24}$ at the projection-noise limit ($λ=100\, μ$m, 95\% C.L.). This is more than three and five orders of magnitude below existing laboratory limits. The improvement covers boson masses of 0.3-50 meV/c$^2$ after the upgrades and 0.09-70 meV/c$^2$ at the projection-noise limit.

title: Spark-0: Scaling Spatially Aligned Tactile Pretraining for Robot Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Tianxing Chen, Wenwei Lin, Chuqiao Lyu, Peicheng Xiang, Junyuan Tang, Tian Nian, Zijian Cai, Kehe Ye, Chenze Yu, Wenxuan Zhu, Eric J. Chen, Yan Qin, Yue Chen, Tongyu Wu, Junhao Gong, Kai-Chong Lei, Jiahao Zhang, Kailun Su, Qiwei Liang, Renjing Xu, Ping Luo, Wenbo Ding
abstract: Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We present Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) model that uses touch in two complementary ways. During pretraining, image-space contact maps derived from tactile gloves, together with features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher, supervise the visual tokens; these objectives are removed at inference. In parallel, a tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states to condition the action expert. A single checkpoint therefore supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment. To scale this supervision, we build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and pretrain Spark-0 on it together with egocentric video, robot data, and simulation. We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Spark-0 achieves the highest mean success rate on both SparkArena tracks and ranks first on all eight aggregate metrics of the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark. Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining. The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty
authors: Chengze Xie, Xuan Wang, Ying Ding, Hairong Wang, Yan Li
abstract: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies.

title: Mem4Act: Learning Effective Latent Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yun Zhang, Zhiyu Huang, Tianhui Cai, Chen Tang, Wei Wang, Jiaqi Ma
abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally requires memory: agents must retain task-relevant information from past observations and interactions and use it to guide future actions. Existing approaches typically preserve raw historical observations, compressed visual tokens, or language summaries, but these representations either expose the action policy to increasingly long histories or risk discarding task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information. We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory as a fixed-size representation explicitly optimized for long-horizon robotic control. Mem4Act addresses three coupled challenges: how to efficiently cover long histories, what information memory should retain, and how to ensure the policy actually relies on memory. To this end, it organizes history via multi-granularity temporal aggregation, preserves complementary semantic and perceptual information through question-answering supervision and key-frame DINO feature reconstruction, and employs memory-first two-stage training to encourage greater use of memory by the action policy. The resulting memory captures both high-level task state and fine-grained perceptual evidence while providing a bounded interface to the action policy. Across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, Mem4Act achieves state-of-the-art performance on memory-dependent control, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%, respectively. Extensive ablations further demonstrate the importance of temporal aggregation, complementary memory supervision, and memory-first training.

title: Differential equations as difference-differential equations
authors: Wei Li, Thomas Scanlon
abstract: We analyze the behavior of systems of algebraic differential equations when considered as systems of difference-differential equations, with special emphasis on systems which define minimal sets relative to the theory $\operatorname{DCF}$ of differentially closed fields of characteristic zero with $m$ distinguished commuting derivations. We show that if $p$ is a minimal type relative to $\operatorname{DCF}$ defined by a system of algebraic partial differential equations and inequations and the forking geometry on $p$ is trivial (also called ``disintegrated''), then $p$ remains minimal when regarded as a partial type relative to the theory $\operatorname{DCFA}$ of difference-differentially closed fields of characteristic zero with $m$ commuting derivations in the sense that every completion has $\operatorname{SU}$-rank one. We illustrate this theorem by describing in detail the possible difference-differential equations consistent with differential equations of the form $y' = y^3 + a_2 y^2 + a_1 y + a_0$ where $a_0$, $a_1$, and $a_2$ are differential constants.

title: MindEval2: Clinically Grounded Patients and Rubrics for Evaluating Language Models in Mental Health Support
authors: John Mendonça, Daniel Tschernutter, José Pombal, Areti Vassilopoulos, Catarina Botelho, Ignacio Sarasua, Maya D'Eon, Nuno Guerreiro, Ricardo Rei
abstract: With people increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, the need to evaluate these tools is becoming more pressing. Recent benchmarks attempt to mimic a realistic setting by simulating multi-turn interactions with synthetic patients and evaluating them with an LLM-as-a-judge. However, the usefulness of these methods is limited because simulated patients can be overly forthcoming and self-reflective, and judgments typically involve opaque Likert scales with unclear practical utility. To bridge these gaps, we introduce MindEval2, an evaluation framework that consists of two components: Mental Health Quality Rubrics (MHQR), for evaluation, and MindSim, for patient simulation. For MHQR, we collaborate with PhD-level psychologists to develop a set of rubrics that break down response quality into explicit operational criteria that are more interpretable and actionable than existing evaluation taxonomies. MindSim, in turn, is an LLM harness that combines carefully-designed patient profiles with tools, enabling more varied, challenging, and realistic interactions than existing baselines. The harness also contains a memory component that is updated between each interaction, enabling MindEval2 to model the longitudinal aspect of mental health. We evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight models on MindEval2, finding that while frontier models have largely improved on issues related to surface level quality and boundaries, guidance calibration remains the dominant failure mode across all models, accounting for most of the quality gap.

title: TraHist: Fast and Accurate Cardinality Estimation for Trajectory Data (Extended Version)
authors: Yujeong Jo, Incheol Baek, Changbeom Shim, Yon Dohn Chung
abstract: Cardinality estimation is fundamental for query optimization in database systems. Histogram-based estimators are widely used for their simplicity and efficiency but rely on point-centric partitioning that assumes record independence. This assumption breaks in trajectory data, where records from the same moving object show strong spatiotemporal dependencies. Conventional axis-aligned histograms therefore fragment trajectories across partition boundaries, leading to overestimation through duplicate counting. This error reflects a structural limitation of partition boundaries that are misaligned with trajectory-induced density patterns. To this end, we propose TraHist, a histogram-based estimator approximating density-aligned partitioning via efficient grid-based propagation. TraHist builds density-adaptive rectilinear buckets to preserve trajectory continuity and local density coherence while keeping histogram efficiency. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets show that TraHist reduces estimation error by over 20x relative to the strongest competing estimator in query regimes where trajectory fragmentation is a dominant source of estimation error, while maintaining sub-millisecond query latency and competitive construction cost.

title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It
authors: Faridoun Mehri, Hinrich Schütze
abstract: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

title: An Induced Subgraph Paradigm for Strongly Regular Graph Constructions
authors: Benjamin Baker
abstract: How many disjoint copies of some graph $H$ can appear in an induced subgraph of a strongly regular graph? We give upper and lower bounds that depend on the number of vertices in their boundary. This generalizes a result of Lou-Murin which bounds the independence number of a (hitherto still elusive) strongly regular graph with parameters $(99,14,1,2)$. The equality cases suggest alternative structural approaches for potential constructions of such a graph. We show, using computer searches, that one cannot impose certain additional natural conditions for some of the cases.

title: Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition in Videos
authors: Jay N. Paranjape, Jurijs Nazarovs, Rohan Sarkar, Yue Guo, Lipeng Ke, Sankar Venkataraman, Vishal M. Patel, Nataraj Jammalamadaka
abstract: Understanding characteristics and activities of individuals in complex multi-person environments is crucial for real-world applications. However, existing datasets often simplify this problem to grounded group activity recognition, single-person activity recognition, or close-set activity recognition, thus limiting the generalizability of models trained on these datasets. In this work, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition (GHADAR), which involves describing the characteristics and activity descriptions of \textbf{every} person in a video, provided the location of the person in the video, which is more practical for real-world applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a new dataset derived from AVA-Actions by generating open-set captions for the person description and activity. In addition, we propose a novel method to effectively utilize the information contained in grounding during training by constraining the cross-attention masks during training in VLMs to improve performance for this task. Our experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA VLMs on this task. Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text-text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a holistic VLM-based evaluation schema that compares concepts {\em directly} between the video and the generated predictions. Thus, in this work, we develop a complete framework for GHADAR, including a dataset, a novel method and an evaluation schema, thereby establishing a strong foundation for future research in this domain.

title: A New Method for Constraining 3D Exoplanet Atmospheres: Application to WASP-94A b's Panchromatic Spectrum
authors: Sagnick Mukherjee, Luis Welbanks, Guangwei Fu, David K. Sing, Michael R. Line
abstract: A growing number of transiting exoplanets exhibit spectroscopic evidence that their leading and trailing limbs differ. Interpreting these observations is now the limiting step. The standard approach of fitting limb-resolved transit depths results in highly anti-correlated transit depths, and treating them as independent measurements can result in strongly biased ($3σ$) retrieved molecular abundances. We present an inference framework that avoids these correlations by using the temporal signature of limb asymmetry instead. This wavelength-dependent shift in mid-transit time, or `time-shift spectrum', carries the limb-asymmetry information, is measurable from existing light curves with a spherically symmetric transit model, and is uncorrelated with the spherically-averaged transit depth. Simultaneously fitting the resulting transmission and time-shift spectrum with an independent atmospheric column for each limb enables the retrieval of limb-resolved properties from two independent measurements. We demonstrate that this approach reduces the mean squared error on the retrieved molecular abundances by factors of $\sim30-50$ relative to next best of the alternative approaches currently adopted in the field, and improves retrieved abundance precision by $\sim3-6\times$. We apply the framework to WASP-94A b and present its panchromatic limb-resolved spectrum, spanning 0.8-5~$μ$m and combining NIRISS/SOSS and NIRSpec/G395H observations. The planet's morning limb remains aerosol-obscured across this entire range, while its evening limb constrains the abundances of H$_2$O, CO$_2$, CO, and H$_2$S. We measure a limb-to-limb temperature difference of $415\pm58$~K at 1~mbar. This limb-resolved analysis finds [M/H]=+0.32$^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and C/O=0.724$^{+0.013}_{-0.013}$, consistent with the host star.

title: Uniform Intersection Numbers and Subgroup-Based Generating Graphs of Groups
authors: Projesh Nath Choudhury, Biswaranjan Khanra
abstract: The uniform intersection number of a finite group $G$, denoted by $ui(G)$, is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that the intersection of any $k$ distinct maximal subgroups of $G$ is equal to its Frattini subgroup. We determine the uniform intersection number of dicyclic, dihedral, and quasi-dihedral groups. We then investigate the uniform intersection number through the subgroup-based generating graph $\mathcal{G}(G)$ of a finite group $G$. We characterize the finite groups $G$ for which both the intersection number and the uniform intersection number are equal to two, and show that this condition is equivalent to $\mathcal{G}(G)$ being complete multipartite. We also classify finite groups in terms of the diameter, girth, and perfectness of $\mathcal{G}(G)$. Finally, we show that $\mathcal{G}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ is Hamiltonian if and only if $n=p_1^{r}p_2^{r}$, where $r\geq 2$ and $p_1$ and $p_2$ are distinct primes.

title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
authors: Shuo Han, Ziqing Hu
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.

title: Local wave-packet spectroscopy of the Drude weight in Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids
authors: Takayuki Yokoyama, Yasuhiro Tada
abstract: We investigate wave packets generated by a local pulse electric field in a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) with a U(1) charge $q$. Bosonization shows that a local pulse field creates two counterpropagating packets with opposite accumulated charges $\pm qK$ and velocity $v$, where $K$ and $v$ are the TLL parameter and velocity. The packet motion produces a linearly growing charge polarization $P(t)=2 qDt$ in the conducting TLL at non-equilibrium, allowing the Drude weight $D=vK$ to be extracted from real-time local dynamics. We test this local-packet description by time-dependent variational principle simulations of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. The simulations visualize the density, current, energy, and entanglement profiles in the space-time plane and confirm the predicted packet charge and propagation velocity. We also show that excess energy and entanglement remaining near the pulse region are suppressed in the weak-pulse limit. Finally, the Drude weight obtained from the packet-induced polarization agrees with the exact Bethe-ansatz result, demonstrating local-packet spectroscopy of intrinsic transport in a TLL.

title: A Sample of Thick-Disk Stars Hosting Hot Jupiters
authors: Victoria DiTomasso, Samuel W. Yee, Romy Rodriguez Martinez, Emily K. Pass, Phillip A. Cargile, David Charbonneau, Andrew Vanderburg, David W. Latham, Vedant Chandra
abstract: We present a homogeneous analysis of 268 confirmed and candidate transiting hot-Jupiter host stars with 4800K < Teff < 6200K. We combine high-resolution TRES spectra, Gaia, 2MASS and WISE photometry, and Gaia astrometry to determine these stars' Teff, log g, Rstar, [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H]. Based on their [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H], we classify the stars as members of the Milky Way's low-[alpha/Fe] thin disk, high-[alpha/Fe] thick disk or an ambiguous intermediate population. We identify two confirmed hot Jupiters (WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b) and three candidate hot Jupiters (TOI-3118.01, TOI-2728.01, and TOI-5781.01) as orbiting previously-unrecognized members of the high-alpha thick disk. We compare the properties of the confirmed planets in the three populations and note two indications of a potential difference between the populations: both high-[alpha/Fe] confirmed planets and eight out of the eleven ambiguous-disk confirmed planets are less massive than the median low-[alpha/Fe] planet, and none of our high-[alpha/Fe] or ambiguous confirmed planets have orbital periods shorter than 2.7 d, when 22% of our low-[alpha/Fe] population do. These differences may reflect variations in giant-planet formation across galactic environments, evolutionary effects, or differing stellar properties between the high- and low-[alpha/Fe] populations. Our catalog is the largest sample of chemically-identified high-[alpha/Fe] thick-disk confirmed and candidate hot-Jupiter host stars. These ancient systems, with ages > 8 Gyr, may allow for a better understanding of how the formation of hot Jupiters depends on galactic environment, and how their orbits evolve over very long time scales.

title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for Long-Horizon Multimodal Search Agents
authors: Huanyao Zhang, Jiepeng Zhou, Jiaye Lin, Ontai Tang, Jingtian Hao, Mugeng Liu, Ru Peng, Lang Mei, Xiaohan Yu, Liyan Liu, Chong Chen, Wentao Zhang
abstract: Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon investigations that continually acquire evidence. However, training such agents remains constrained by limited challenging training questions and insufficient process feedback. We introduce MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline performs targeted expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple multimodal questions. Parameterized transformations control search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing existing image--question pairs. For training, answer rewards and lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect student trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient reduces teacher dependence as training proceeds. Experiments show gains from data refinement and further improvements from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities.

title: Observing minimal submanifolds with isolated singularities on open sets of metrics
authors: Alessandro Carlotto, Yangyang Li, Zhihan Wang
abstract: We develop a perturbative theory for minimal submanifolds with only (strongly) isolated singularities, with respect to varying background Riemannian metrics. As an application, we obtain a general "sporadic persistence" criterion, thus naturally complementing the non-persistence theorem by the authors. In particular, such a criterion is satisfied by the spherical suspension in $\mathbb{S}^{3m+2}$ of the Veronese embedding of $\mathbb{K}\mathbb{P}^2$ for $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H},\mathbb{O}$ (the normed division algebras) in the round spheres of dimension $3m+1=4,7,13,25$ respectively, thereby providing families of continuously varying $(2m+1)$-dimensional stationary varifolds with isolated singularities that are observable on an open set of metrics. By our previous results, these phenomena cannot possibly occur in the codimension one scenario.

title: Variation of Shafarevich-Tate groups in Hida families
authors: Enrico Da Ronche, Matteo Longo, Stefano Vigni, Francesco Zerman
abstract: Let $\mathbf{f}$ be a Hida family of cusp forms over a standard (power series) Iwasawa algebra. We determine the pseudo-isomorphism class of the big Shafarevich-Tate group attached to $\mathbf{f}$ over a suitable imaginary quadratic field by describing all its higher Fitting ideals; this description is given in terms of the universal Kolyvagin system of Howard's big Heegner points. As a second contribution, we study the variation of the structure of the Shafarevich-Tate groups of the classical specializations of $\mathbf{f}$.

title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
authors: Angus Crookes, Ben Yuen, Angela Demetriadou
abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

title: Gallium Anomaly and Solar Neutrinos
authors: Steven R. Elliott, R. G. Hamish Robertson
abstract: The Gallium Anomaly is the disagreement between the measured capture rate of neutrinos by $^{71}$Ga and the rate theoretically expected from the electron capture decay of $^{71}$Ge. The experimental measurements were performed with intense artificial sources. In the present work we consider the sun as a neutrino source that can be calibrated via the fundamental, standard-model neutrino-electron elastic scattering reaction in terrestrial detectors. The result is found to be not anomalous, with good agreement between the measured value of $66.1\pm3.1$ SNU from SAGE and Gallex/GNO, and the total measured source strengths of solar sources, $67.5^{+1.4}_{-1.1}$ SNU. It may be concluded that neither the $^{71}$Ga charged-current cross section nor gallium experiment extraction and counting efficiencies account for the Gallium Anomaly.

title: GNN-Guided Local Refinement for Efficient Layout Decomposition with DSA-MP
authors: Yu Feng, Liyi Zhou, Haoyu Wang, Yiming Xu, Hao Geng, Shaozhi Deng, Ningsheng Xu, Shisheng Xiong
abstract: Multiple patterning lithography (MPL) has been widely used to improve lithography resolution in advanced nodes, but it faces cost limits as feature sizes shrink. Directed self-assembly (DSA) offers a cost-effective complement, extending the resolution of optical lithography to sub-10 nm and beyond. Integrating DSA into MPL (DSA-MP) further enhances the resolution of contact/via patterning. Nevertheless, growing design complexity exposes the limits of existing decomposition methods, which struggle to balance solution quality and runtime, and neglect edge-to-edge spacing constraints of DSA templates, compromising manufacturability. To address these issues, we introduce a new conflict graph model capturing the previously overlooked constraints and develop a local refinement strategy powered by the graph neural network, enabling efficient and scalable layout decomposition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher solution quality with faster convergence than state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robustness across layout scales, design styles, technology nodes, and varying mask counts.

title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
authors: Eduardo Dueñez, José Iovino
abstract: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

title: Series of Fano quiver moduli from extended Dynkin quivers
authors: Pieter Belmans, Markus Reineke
abstract: Associated to small extended Dynkin quivers, we construct series of Fano varieties of fixed Picard rank at most five and arbitrary even dimension, which admit a very explicit description of their geometry. For example, they all admit a flat morphism to a projective space, whose general fiber is a product of projective lines. We also give a closed formula for all Betti numbers, and interpret this formula in terms of an action of a cohomological Hall algebra on the cohomology of all the varieties in a series.

title: Properties and limitations of linear models for mutual coupling in 21 cm arrays
authors: Vincent MacKay, Robert Pascua, Eleanor Rath, Jacqueline N. Hewitt, Tyler Cox, Nicholas Kern, Joshua S. Dillon, Aaron Parsons, Eloy de Lera Acedo, Nicolas Fagnoni
abstract: Mutual coupling between elements of low-frequency arrays is a leading systematic for 21 cm cosmology, leaking bright foregrounds into otherwise clean regions of the power spectrum. Many mitigation models describe coupling as a linear combination of uncoupled signals re-radiated from neighboring feeds, but data suggest additional mechanisms. Inspired by antenna scattering theory, we decompose coupling into an antenna mode, constructed from translated isolated responses and expected to be removable by linear combination models, and a structural mode, the remainder. Full-wave simulations of HERA-like feeds and dishes in a 37-element hexagonal array show that the antenna mode accounts for only about 1% of the beam perturbation power, suggesting limited scope for mitigation with linear models. Two effects nevertheless lead to substantially better suppression. First, correlating beams and weighting them by the sky changes the modes' relative importance: correcting the antenna mode can remove more than half of the coupling power in simulated visibilities. Second, relaxing the coefficient relationships imposed by re-radiation allows linear corrections to remove structural-mode coupling too. Beam-derived corrections can reduce coupling power by over an order of magnitude in our noiseless simulations of perfectly redundant arrays. Fitting directly to known isolated visibilities reduces residuals further on the fitted field, but this target is generally unavailable in observations. Practical correction therefore requires additional constraints to separate the unknown sky from coupling while preserving the cosmological signal. We introduce an extension of holographic back-projection to coupled beams, providing an intuitive picture of these perturbations in the aperture plane.

title: Terminal-RSI: Recursive Self-Improving Terminal Agents via Recursive Self-Rewrite and Policy-Refine
authors: Junyao Yang, Zongxia Li, Yucheng Shi, Zhongzhi Li, Ruhan Wang, Ruiwen Zhou, Haitao Mi, Shuicheng Yan, Leowei Liang
abstract: Converting verifier outcomes into useful policy updates and partial progress into complete task resolution is crucial for terminal agents. We present Terminal-RSI, which alternates Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR) of verified trajectories with critic-inheriting Recursive Policy-Refine (RPR). We formulate Turn-Boundary Skip-Observation GAE (TB-GAE) to retain token-specific baselines while applying decay across interaction turns. Family Dense Reward (FDR) calibrates semantic progress across task families; Success-Prioritized Reward (SPR) separates strict success from bounded partial credit. A Warm-up Critic Model, recursive critic handoff, and stage-specific learning rates coordinate the two refinement phases. The five-stage sequence from Qwen3.8-27B base model through RSR-1, RPR-1, RSR-2, and RPR-2 yields Terminal-RSI-27B: 19.84% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 86.52% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 16.95% on Terminal-Bench 3.0, and 79.00% on Terminal-Bench Hard. On LHTB, process reward rises from 0.21 to 0.37 and strict completion from 0/46 to 5/46; SWR100 success doubles from 3.00% to 6.00%. By recursively coupling verified trajectory rewriting with critic-inheriting policy refinement, each retained stage consolidates discovered behaviors and progressively advances the agent from partial local repairs to strict terminal verification.

title: Stable topology and stable compactness
authors: Tiexin Guo, Qiang Tu, Xiaohuan Mu, Goong Chen, Pasqualetto Enrico, Guang Yang
abstract: To solve a large class of noncompact problems ubiquitous in random functional analysis and its applications, most of compactness-based fundamental theorems established for normed spaces or locally convex spaces are required to be extended for random normed modules and random locally convex modules in an appropriate way of weakening compactness. To achieve this goal, in this paper we first develop stable set theory by introducing some new set-theoretic tools, then propose a class of topological spaces with a stable structure, called stable topological spaces, and in particular propose and systematically develop the theory of stably compact spaces, which is a natural generalization of that of compact spaces. The resulting theory is of independent interest from the perspective of general topology since its investigation requires an analysis of stratification structures coordinated with partitions of unity in a complete Boolean algebra. Finally, we show the power of the theory of stable compactness by establishing random Banach-Alaoglu, random James and random Banach-Bourbaki-Kakutani-Šmulian theorems.

title: Whole-Body Dexterity
authors: Conor Mc Gartoll, An Dang, Pranay Thangeda, Arjun Gupta, Carolina Higuera, Nima Fazeli, Mustafa Mukadam, Manikantan Nambi
abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz Böhle
abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.

title: Inertially Significant Humanoid Teleoperation via Whole Body Model Predictive Control and Online Parameter Estimation
authors: James Foster, Beomyeong Park, Luigi Penco, Robert Griffin
abstract: The effective deployment of humanoid robots in practical tasks of interest will require a capability of sensing and adapting to variations in inertial parameters, as occurs during heavy tool use or when carrying significant payload. Such payloads constitute a significant proportion of the combined payload-robot system, the effects of which cannot be ignored by delegating to feedback control. This paper showcases a general solution to this problem by integrating a whole body model predictive controller (WB-MPC) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for online estimation of fully physically consistent time-varying inertial parameters. These estimates are fed through to the WB-MPC's full rigid body dynamics model, resulting in more accurate feedforward torques for task demands under external load. Additionally, a virtual reality (VR) interface is provided that enables an operator to provide task-specific references without regard to payload while delegating dynamic balance to the WB-MPC. The framework is validated with simulation and hardware experiments on a humanoid system.

title: Cone Invariance and Homoclinic Standing Waves for Cooperative Finite-Range DNLS Equations
authors: Vassilios M. Rothos
abstract: We develop a constrained-power variational framework for positive homoclinic standing waves in one-dimensional discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equations with cooperative finite-range interactions. Starting from periodic lattices, we construct constrained energy maximizers and use the associated projected gradient flow to establish positive invariance of the cone of nonnegative, even, and unimodal profiles. A central result is that the monotone ordering of the interaction coefficients, \(a_1\ge a_2\ge\cdots\ge a_M\ge0\), with \(a_1>0\), provides the structural condition ensuring preservation of this cone under finite-range coupling. Under a strict maximum condition above the linear spectral edge, we obtain a uniform frequency gap and period-independent exponential localization. These estimates provide the compactness required for the infinite-period limit and yield positive, even, unimodal, and exponentially localized homoclinic standing waves as strong \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\)-limits of periodic constrained maximizers. Numerical computations for several interaction ranges and cooperative kernels illustrate the effects of extended coupling on dispersion and localization and support the periodic-to-homoclinic convergence predicted by the analysis.

title: EMO: A Closed-Loop Test-Time Computation Framework via Alternating Context Optimization and Logits Steering
authors: Wei Xia, Yehui Tang, Zhi-Hong Deng
abstract: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation--maximization that alternates question-specific context estimation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions under the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging $+9.10$ percentage points. With the same judge, it adds $+1.53$ points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-$N$ are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates. The coverage--selection gap motivates allocating test-time computation jointly to candidate generation and verification.

title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
authors: Jingyu Tang, Xu Yang, Zhehao Zhang, Zheng Wang, Qi Cheng, Haozhe Zhao, Manling Li, Wenxuan Li, Xide Xia, Jiaxin Pei
abstract: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. These findings suggest directions for improving real-time multimodal agents, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action.

title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference, and make the latency guarantee layered and explicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k-frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occupancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their software references. On the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set the board reaches mIoU 29.88, 92.8% of an FP32 baseline the DPU cannot run. On a ResNet-50 probe over 100k frames the KR260 tail stays within 1.5 times its median (2.0 times for the six-inference proxy), where Jetson Orin reaches 4.4 times and the worst datacenter GPU run (NVIDIA L4) 23.6 times. The deployment recipe, HLS sources, and raw timing traces are released.

title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions
authors: Liangjie Huang, Henry Peng Zou, Wei-Chieh Huang, Wooseong Yang, Yuwei Han, Philip S. Yu
abstract: LLM systems increasingly rely on groups of agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, assuming that peers will catch individual errors. We test this assumption against a minimal adversary. In a ten-agent factual discussion, one or three adversarial agents repeatedly assert a plausible false answer. After each round we probe each benign agent's private answer through a separate call whose response is hidden from its peers, and we separately label its public stance toward the claim. Across six models and three factual-QA datasets, groups remain stable without an attacker: only 0.6% of benign agents finish with the false answer. A single adversarial agent increases this rate to 44.8% and three to 60.5%. Studies of conformity typically report public agreement without private change; we find the reverse. With three adversarial agents present, benign agents hold the false answer in 51.6% of exposed turns but publicly endorse it in only 19.7%. Much of the influence therefore remains invisible in the discussion, and the false answers persist when agents are asked for their own views. Agents that retain the true answer often fail to defend it; once adopted, the false answer spreads among benign agents, and baseline knowledge does not predict robustness.

title: Unimodular Zeros of Selmer's Harmonic Trinomials
authors: Gerardo Barrera, Waldemar Barrera, Juan Pablo Navarrete
abstract: Let $n>k$ be positive integers and let $\varepsilon,δ\in\{-1,1\}$. In this note, we classify the unimodular zeros of the harmonic trinomial $H_{\varepsilon,δ}:\mathbb{C}\to \mathbb{C}$ given by \[ H_{\varepsilon,δ}(z)=z^n+\varepsilon\overline z^{\,k}+δ, \] where $\overline{z}$ is the complex conjugate of $z\in \mathbb{C}$. Let $g:=\gcd(n,k)$ be the greatest common divisor of $n$ and $k$, and set $n_0:=n/g$ and $k_0:=k/g$. For each choice of $\varepsilon,δ\in \{-1,1\}$, we give a necessary and sufficient congruence involving $n_0$ and $k_0$ to guarantee that $H_{\varepsilon,δ}$ has unimodular zeros. More precisely, if the corresponding congruence holds, then $H_{\varepsilon,δ}$ has exactly $2g$ unimodular zeros, which are given explicitly; otherwise, it has no unimodular zeros. The proof uses a reduction to a trinomial equation and elementary divisibility arguments.

title: Rovibrational cross sections for the CO$_2$ $00^00$, $01^10$, $02^20$ and Fermi resonance states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$ in collisions with He atoms
authors: Jelena Bošković, Taha Selim, Ad van der Avoird, Floris F. S. van der Tak, Gerrit C. Groenenboom
abstract: We present quantum scattering calculations of CO$_2$-He state-to-state integral cross sections for 25 transition sets, covering pure rotational transitions within and rovibrational transitions between: the ground state $00^00$, the bend fundamental $01^10$, the bending overtone $02^20$, and the Fermi doublet states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$. Exact coupled-channel (CC) and coupled-states approximation (CSA) calculations are performed using a new five-dimensional potential energy surface. The calculations cover collision energies from 20 to 5220 cm$^{-1}$, sufficient to obtain converged rate coefficients over 100-800 K, and include initial rotational states for each transition up to at least $j=35$. We present an energy-grid algorithm for rovibrational quantum scattering calculations that minimizes the number of separate calculations required. The resulting cross sections exhibit a dominant $Δj=0$ propensity and parity-dependent patterns. For the benchmark $00^00,j' \leftarrow 01^10,j$ transition, thermally averaged rate coefficients reproduce available experimental data. A comparison between the CC and CSA cross sections shows that, for vibrational quenching transitions, the CSA cross sections increasingly deviate from the CC results with increasing initial rotational state $j$. Calculated integral cross sections cover collision energies and rotational states needed to derive rate coefficients for non local thermal equilibrium radiative transfer modeling of mid-infrared CO$_2$ spectra. The computationally simpler CO$_2$-He system allows the methodology and approximations to be tested at high collision energies and rotational states, helping assess their suitability for the more complex and astrochemically important CO$_2$-H$_2$ system.

title: An undecidable problem in dynamics
authors: Jason Bell
abstract: Given a variety $X$ with a self-map $φ$ and subvarieties $Y$ and $Z$ of $X$, we consider the set of $n$ for which $φ^n(Y)$ intersects $Z$ nontrivially. Extending a beautiful construction of Lee and Nam, we show this gives rise to an undecidable problem for a fixed ambient variety $X$ and morphism $φ$. We further use this construction to give a counterexample to a conjecture of the author, Satriano, and Sierra.

title: Polarizable quasiconvex function generated metric projection
authors: A. B. Németh, S. Z. Németh
abstract: We study when generalized metric projections generated by strongly quasiconvex functions are polarizable. The point of departure is Moreau's decomposition theorem, where the Euclidean metric projections onto two mutually polar closed convex cones form complementary retractions whose sum is the identity. This suggests the following fundamental question: when does a given retraction admit such a complementary polar retraction? We formulate this notion through polarizable retractions and then specialize it to generalized projections of the form $x\mapsto P_{\cal C}^\varphi(x)$, defined by minimizing $\varphi(x-y)$ with respect to $y$ over a closed convex set ${\cal C}$. After recalling basic properties of mutually polar retractions and first-order characterizations of generalized projections, we prove the main result: If $\varphi$ is strongly quasiconvex, the generalized projection $P_{\cal C}^\varphi$ is polarizable if and only if ${\cal C}$ is a closed convex cone. Thus, polarizability of the projection is characterized by the conic geometry of its range.

title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
authors: Nicolás Vera Zúñiga
abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.

title: The Radius-Luminosity Relationship for Active Galactic Nuclei with Hierarchical Bayesian Reverberation Mapping
authors: Hugh McDougall, Tamara M. Davis, Benjamin J. S. Pope, Paul Martini, Zhefu Yu, Chris Lidman, Geraint F. Lewis, Christian Adamcewicz, Rahma Alfarsy
abstract: Reverberation mapping of active galactic nuclei uses the time taken for variability to travel through the system as a measure of system size, with this size being used to inform estimates of the mass of the central black hole, a technique that has graduated to an industrial-scale effort in recent decades. Such large target-count, multi-year surveys have been consistently undercut by poor light curve quality and the aliasing problems of seasonal observations. These impacts compound with statistical approaches that are not consistent between works and sometimes combine inconsistent statistical frameworks. Here, we present a new end-to-end Bayesian framework for fitting lags at scale in large surveys, simultaneous with the fitting of population models such as the radius-luminosity relation, and formulated in a numerically tractable way. This procedure is a statistically and numerically robust generalisation of the stacking and quality cut procedures of past works, fully marginalising over data uncertainty and data quality. Our approach remains numerically stable when scaling to larger surveys, and can act as a basis for any Bayesian population modelling of large sets of AGN time series observations. Applied to the OzDES sample, we demonstrate that this new approach yields more than double the constraining power on population-level properties like the R-L relationship, and an order-of-magnitude increase in the number of recovered lags and masses. With this method, we go from 24 high quality lag recoveries with traditional methods to a new effective sample size of ~297, all while being robust against random chance false positive measurements.

title: Global strong solutions without contact for a viscous fluid interacting with a purely elastic beam
authors: Yadong Liu
abstract: We consider a two-dimensional incompressible viscous fluid confined in a periodic channel between a fixed flat wall and a purely elastic periodic beam. For compatible initial fluid velocity in $H^1$, beam height in $H^3$, and beam velocity in $H^1$, with strictly positive initial height, we establish global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions. In particular, there is no contact of the beam and bottom, which is built on a uniform distance bound derived by the mechanical energy and fluid dissipation through a height-dependent degenerate elliptic regularization of the classical distance test. Combining tangential differentiation, a fractional estimate for the height, and a negative-order tangential estimate for the accelerations, we establish a global regularity estimate. Moreover, quadratic time-weighted estimates that quantify the higher regularity at positive times are justified. As a consequence, the work gives an affirmative answer to the problem proposed by Grandmont and Hillairet (Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 220(3): 1283--1333, 2016) of whether fluid dissipation alone is sufficient to derive the distance estimate.

title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following
authors: Daniela Baiamonte, Kamyar Zeinalipour, Elena Fano, Stefano Simonazzi, Andrea Zugarini
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.

title: Logarithmic exponential sums with multiplicative coefficients
authors: Haozhe Gou
abstract: Let $f$ be a $1$-bounded multiplicative function, and suppose that $|α-a/q|\leq 1/(qx)$, where $(a,q)=1$ and $q\leq x$. We prove that $$ \left|\sum_{n\leq x}\frac{f(n)}{n}e( nα)\right| \leq \left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}+o(1)\right)\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{q}}+O(\log q). $$ Here the constant $4/\sqrt{6}$ is optimal. This settles two conjectures of Granville and Lamzouri recently. If $f$ is completely multiplicative, the constant improves to $1$. The main new ingredient is a two-prime Ramaré decomposition identity.

title: Quantitative vanishing-regularization limits for degenerate cross-diffusion with changing boundary strata
authors: E. Yu. Shchetinin, A. A. Shevchuk, S. I. Salpagarov
abstract: We study a vanishing-regularization limit for a degenerate cross-diffusion system on the simplex when the active boundary stratum of a smooth reference solution may change in space and time. The mobility $M(u)=\operatorname{diag}u-u\otimes u$ loses rank when a component vanishes, so a fixed relative entropy or an unweighted two-point gradient estimate cannot remain uniformly coercive across moving faces. We introduce a geometric-relative framework that separates the single emerging normal direction from the active tangential subsystem. Its ingredients are a global resolvent geodesic distance, a boundary-oriented rank-one perspective correction, an intrinsic Schur-normal De Giorgi alternative, a mean-free tangential iteration with temporal-flux control, and a terminal coupled Schur compactness argument. These mechanisms yield a non-circular first-exit theorem for smooth approximations and then pass to admissibly approximable entropy weak solutions. If the strong solution stays a fixed distance from the codimension-two skeleton and its vanishing components satisfy $|\nabla v_i|\lesssim v_i^α$ and $|\{0<v_i<r\}|\lesssim r^σ$, then the augmented relative energy is bounded by $ρ_λ=λ^{2α+σ}$ if $2α+σ<2$, $ρ_λ=λ^2|\logλ|$ if $2α+σ=2$, and $ρ_λ=λ^2$ if $2α+σ>2$. For a hypersurface contact $v_i\asymp d^p$, $p\ge2$, this gives $ρ_λ=O(λ^{2-1/p})$ and $\|u^λ-v\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^2)}=O(λ^{1-1/(2p)})$.

title: Direct products of Gorenstein flat modules over coherent rings
authors: Guocheng Dai, Jiangsheng Hu
abstract: We construct a commutative coherent local algebra of Krull dimension zero and a countably generated projectively coresolved Gorenstein flat module whose countable power has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension. This answers negatively the question of whether Gorenstein flat modules over a right coherent ring are closed under direct products. As a consequence, we obtain a pure-injective Ding injective module whose character module has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension and whose character bidual has infinite Gorenstein injective dimension. We also give equivalent conditions for Gorenstein flat modules over a right coherent ring to be closed under direct products, in terms of relative Mittag--Leffler conditions, stationarity, and Gorenstein flat and injective dimensions of character biduals. For the constructed ring, we exhibit a decreasing countable sequence of strong submodules of a free module whose intersection has infinite Gorenstein flat dimension. Thus the abstract elementary class of Gorenstein flat modules, with the strong submodule relation, has finite character but does not admit intersections.

title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
authors: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.

title: CBF-Based Control Allocation for Omnidirectional Tiltrotor Aerial Robots
authors: Seobeom Lee, Hyondong Oh
abstract: Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve. Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs. A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%. These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.

title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms
authors: Mohamed Khair, Junpei Komiyama
abstract: In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase. At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR's worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure $H_1(P)$ is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR's performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths. We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent. Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call $H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects ($H_1$-SR). This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules. For Gaussian arms with common variance, $H_1$-SR achieves at least $11/12$ of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every $K\ge2$, and this approximation ratio converges to one as $1-O(1/\log K)$ as $K\to\infty$. This is a significant improvement over original SR, whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to $1/4$. Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.
