title: Napoleonic triangles on the sphere from similar chord triangles
authors: Quang Hung Tran
abstract: We study a variant of Napoleon's construction on the unit sphere, in which the triangles erected on the sides of a spherical triangle $ABC$ are required to have similar isosceles chord triangles with apex angle $β\in(0,π/2)$. For a non-equilateral $ABC$, we prove that the triangle $XYZ$ of spherical circumcentres is equilateral if and only if $\cos(θ_a+θ_b+θ_c\pmΩ/2)=0$, where $θ_a,θ_b,θ_c$ are the base angles of the isosceles spherical triangles $XBC$, $YCA$, $ZAB$, $Ω$ is the area of $ABC$, and the sign $+$ (resp.~$-$) corresponds to the outward (resp.~inward) construction. We derive from this an explicit classification in terms of two quadrics and a cubic inequality. It recovers the theorem of Dipierro, Noakes and Valdinoci for $β=π/3$, and exhibits three families of solutions for $β>π/3$, together with a fourth one when $\cosβ<1/4$.

title: MemCut: Every Secret Leaves a Trail in the Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
authors: Cheng Zhang, Xuanning Cao, Zhicheng Zheng, Hui Xiong
abstract: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of large language model (LLM) agents, with most research focusing on retrieving relevant information accurately and efficiently. However, a dependable memory system must also forget sensitive user data upon request. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MemCut, a systematic benchmark for user-requested forgetting. Its 456 hand-designed secrets in long-horizon conversations have fully annotated evidence trails to test recovery after deletion, including from messages that never state the secrets directly. We propose two recovery metrics. Native recovery measures reader success through the system's retrieval, whereas residual recovery measures the same reader's success when directly given surviving objects traced to annotated disclosures or evidence. We establish three reference deletion baselines to test how far existing retrievers and write models support forgetting across five memory designs and four LLMs. Disclosure removal reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery. LLM-guided deletion of ten additional turns from twenty retrieval candidates leaves 39-76% residual recovery. Subset sweeps (144 facts, three systems, two models) show that widening the pool at a fixed budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates. These sweeps identify candidate coverage as a bottleneck in the reference baselines.

title: Multi-Reward Hacking: From Aggregation-Induced Drift to Trust-Anchored Defense
authors: Yushu Li, Jiin Woo, Xiaoxiao Li, Youngsuk Park
abstract: To improve task performance while encouraging desirable response properties, LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with auxiliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency). However, how these rewards are aggregated can critically affect training outcomes. We show that symmetric aggregation, which treats reward channels equally, can induce a failure where aggregate reward improves while primary-task performance degrades, even when individual rewards are meaningful. We investigate this aggregation-induced failure through a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, characterizing when it constitutes multi-reward hacking. We prove that, under symmetric aggregation, deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. We propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor channel based on the policy drift induced by optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on anchor satisfaction. Unlike calibration-sensitive static reweighting, TAG structurally eliminates credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit for joint success. In the same analytical setting, TAG provably reverses this selection, converging to the primary-favoring action from any initialization when the primary channel is anchored. Experiments across Qwen and Llama models on mathematics and program synthesis reveal substantial degradation under symmetric, constrained, and normalized aggregation, whereas TAG mitigates this failure. On Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, TAG achieves 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation, while shortening responses by 44% relative to correctness-only training.

title: Climate Physicalization: Bridging Tangible Interaction and Data Visualization for Environmental Communication
authors: Milena Vuckovic, Marlene Huber, Fabrizia Bando-Bechtold, Daniel Cornel, Daniel Pahr
abstract: Raising awareness of climate topics, such as urban heat mitigation, requires communicating complex data to a broad audience. Data physicalization has emerged as a novel method to connect audiences to such complex topics through tangible forms while also leveraging interactivity to foster deeper engagement. This paper introduces an situated geospatial thermal physicalization prototype, designed to enhance communication and education of environmental information through hands-on engagement. The physical model depicts a 3D model of an urban neighborhood, with radiation data represented as a layered contour structure. The model incorporates three interchangeable climate adaptation scenarios, alongside an externally mounted, electronically driven solar path representation featuring multiple discrete LEDs that can be switched on and off at will. To investigate how people engage with the model, we conducted a hands-on qualitative lab study with 16 participants, using think-aloud, observational, and questionnaire protocols. Overall, participants responded very favorably to the model, highlighting the novelty of the visualization approach and its capacity to improve the interpretability of the presented information.

title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.

title: CoDeFont: One-Shot Font Generation via Multi-Scale Factor-Specific Representation Learning
authors: Rejoy Chakraborty, Prasun Roy, Saumik Bhattacharya, Umapada Pal
abstract: One-shot Font Generation (OFG) aims to synthesize a target glyph by transferring the stylistic characteristics of a single reference glyph while preserving the structure of the target character. However, accurately capturing font style from a single reference image remains challenging due to the limited stylistic information available in a single glyph, and this challenge is further amplified for complex scripts. We propose CoDeFont, a script-agnostic OFG framework that addresses this challenge through multi-level style-content factorization and progressive style-content reconciliation. CoDeFont independently aggregates complementary style and structural information across multiple spatial levels to obtain factor-specific representations, while a contrastive objective explicitly encourages separation between style and content embeddings. During reconstruction, the disentangled representations are progressively injected through multi-level style conditioning, enabling stylistic information to be incorporated at different decoding resolutions while preserving the underlying glyph structure. We evaluate CoDeFont on structurally distinct Bengali and Latin scripts across seen and unseen font styles. Extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed framework for OFG across diverse writing systems.

title: Two Sample Sizes in Test-Time LLM Ensembling: Buffered ERM and Minimax Theory
authors: Zhi Zhang, Arash A. Amini
abstract: Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: $Q$ labeled questions and $N$ generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's infinite-generation voting rule. Under a margin condition with exponent $β$, we show that empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a calibrated margin buffer achieves excess risk of order $Q^{-1/2}+N^{-β/2}$, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed numbers of models and candidate answers. To investigate the optimality of this dependence on $Q$ and $N$, we analyze a simplified submodel with two models and two possible answers per question. We characterize its minimax excess risk up to constants by a Hellinger modulus for a binomial-mixture experiment. Polynomial approximation and spectral analysis reveal three regimes. When questions are relatively scarce, the $Q^{-1/2}$ term governs learning and the general buffered ERM is optimal. In an intermediate regime, pooling generation counts across questions improves upon estimating each answer distribution separately, with only logarithmic gains from additional questions. With sufficiently many questions, the minimax excess risk reaches an $N^{-β}$ identification floor that persists even with infinitely many questions. The submodel's lower bounds also apply to general ensembles, matching the buffered-ERM upper bound up to logarithmic factors when questions are scarce and in parts of the intermediate regime. Questions remain about the transitions between regimes and the construction of matching pooled estimators for general ensembles.

title: Hierarchical Building-Floo-Room Framework for Privacy-Preserving Autonomous Delivery in Large-Scale Buildings
authors: Xu Xiaoji, Luo Rui, Chen Jinhua, Xiang Changying, Zhang Leihan, Liao Zhongyuan
abstract: Autonomous delivery in large scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building-Floor-Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter building and inter floor connectivity, room level access constraints, and privacy sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non interactive, privacy preserving delivery, supported by reachability aware distances and a closed loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.

title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate via Model-Agnostic Importance Measures
authors: Mengtao Wen, Haojie Ren, Changliang Zou
abstract: Selecting covariates while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) is critical for interpretable scientific discovery, especially with complex machine learning models. Traditional variable selection methods often rely on specific model assumptions, while Model-X knockoffs provide a general way that leverages knowledge of the covariate distribution to produce a variable selection algorithm. This study puts forward a complementary method to Model-X knockoffs, named Model-Agnostic Selection with agent-X importance (MAS), which utilizes the sample-splitting strategy and a novel variable importance measure to bypass distributional assumptions on covariates. The proposed model-agnostic agent-X importance is defined to evaluate the difference of oracle predictiveness on both the original distribution and the distribution with agent variable in population level, and can be efficiently estimated by constructing the agent variable as some constant and cross-fitting strategy. The MAS method integrates a resplit-per-covariate strategy to decouple estimator dependencies and a data aggregation technique to enhance power. Theoretical guarantees for asymptotic FDR control are established under mild conditions. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate that MAS provides competitive performances with existing works in FDR control, computational efficiency and power.

title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
authors: Anh-Van Vu, Changmin Sung, Dongsoo Han
abstract: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs. To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module. It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I2C, SPI, UART). Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions. The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA). Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise. By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.

title: OpCredit: Operation-Aware Policy Learning for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
authors: Yucheng Li, Mingyuan Li, Xiaxia Wang, Gong Cheng
abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering(KGQA) relies on sequences of executable operations, but trajectory-level rewards obscure their individual contributions. Successful trajectories may contain ineffective operations, while failed trajectories may contain useful ones. To assess individual operations, we propose OpCredit, an operationaware policy-learning framework that combines downstream outcome credit with immediate transition credit: Branch Outcome Credit (BOC) reuses ordinary rollouts to compare terminal task rewards observed after different operations under matched navigation contexts; Frontier Transition Credit (FTC) measures operation-induced changes in answer-conditioned frontier potential. The two complementary signals jointly supervise the corresponding decision spans during training, while inference uses only the learned policy and standard KG interface. Experiments on ComplexWebQuestions, WebQSP, and GrailQA across three backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in KGQA performance.

title: Higher-order necessary conditions for nonscattering
authors: Narek Hovsepyan
abstract: We study the scattering of incident waves by a class of planar analytic inhomogeneities with constant refractive index, governed by the Helmholtz equation. We derive an infinite hierarchy of necessary conditions for nonscattering: any complex analytic nonscattering incident wave must satisfy infinitely many differential constraints at a specific point determined by the geometry of the inhomogeneity. As an application, we show that for any noncircular elliptical inhomogeneity, every single separated (Mathieu) mode necessarily scatters. This is in stark contrast to the circular case, where single separated (Bessel) modes are nonscattering at infinitely many wavenumbers.

title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
authors: Yufan Zhu, Yangfan Jiang, Yang Fei, Shizheng Hou, Shubhankar Mohapatra, Xiaokui Xiao
abstract: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.

title: Semantic Latent Alignment for Flow Matching with Invertible Bi-Lipschitz Adapters
authors: Felix Nützel, Mischa Dombrowski, Luca Hagen, Bernhard Kainz
abstract: Pretrained latent spaces trade compression, reconstruction, and the learnability of the coordinates a downstream generator has to work in, which complicates adapting these spaces to different domains or tasks: continued training is expensive, and without a new alignment objective it often fails to improve downstream generation. We instead leave the encoder and decoder fixed and change only the coordinates between them, using an invertible bi-Lipschitz adapter aligned offline to a semantic teacher and frozen during class-conditional flow matching. Invertibility preserves compatibility with the pretrained autoencoder, while the bi-Lipschitz constraint limits how far alignment can distort its latent geometry. This provides a simple way to improve semantic organization while retaining the compression and reconstruction properties of the original latent space. On two medical imaging datasets, constrained latent adaptation improves feature metrics, seed stability and counterfactual edit strength, while remaining competitive on downstream classification. In contrast, unconstrained adaptation can become highly anisotropic and sensitive despite remaining invertible, highlighting the importance of controlling geometric distortion. Our results suggest that carefully constrained post-hoc adaptation offers a parameter-efficient and tuning-free alternative to jointly modifying the representation during generative training.

title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine Optimization on Electoral Visibility
authors: Shiqi Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for election information, yet little is known about how external web content shapes the political information they present. Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content to improve its visibility in generated responses. To investigate its potential risks in voting scenarios (VoteGEO), we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark covering the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2026 Japanese House of Representatives election, combining election-related queries, historical webpages, and voter personas. We first analyze sources cited by generative engines and find that many citations come from lower-cost owned and open-platform sources, while some webpages remain visible across days. We then evaluate 11 rewriting strategies in 4 categories, examining target specification, effectiveness across engines and elections, and the role of voter personas. Rewriting without specifying a target rarely increases target exposure, whereas target-specified rewriting more often does. Strategies that improve page organization or strengthen a position through argumentation yield greater gains than adding supporting evidence or changing wording. For the two strongest strategies, gains remain broadly positive across evaluated U.S. personas, but persona conditioning shows no consistent effect on these gains. Explicit partisan identities can create baseline exposure gaps larger than the gain from rewriting one webpage. When partisanship is implicit in the voter profile, baseline shifts depend on how strongly the engine responds to that signal.

title: RAT-EC: Introducing a New Open-Source 3D Volume-Integral Eddy-Current Module
authors: Daniel Mayr, Jeroen van Nugteren, Julien Dular, Mariusz Wozniak, Jasmin Smajic, Juerg Leuthold
abstract: We present RAT-EC, an open-source volume-integral eddy-current module for unstructured meshes, driven in the time domain by coils of arbitrary winding geometry. It is the first openly available code of this kind and part of the open-source RAT suite. Because only the conductor is meshed, neither the surrounding air nor an artificial outer boundary has to be modelled, which simplifies model preparation and brings problems with thin gaps and intricate air regions within reach of standard hardware. The formulation combines a semi-analytical evaluation of the singular and near-singular inductance terms, a multi-level fast multipole method that accelerates both the far-field inductance action and the coil field, topology-aware constraints for multiply connected conductors, and a matrix-free, GPU-accelerated time integration. The implementation is verified against closed-form solutions for a conducting sphere and a conducting ring, and is validated on the TEAM-7 benchmark. At 50 Hz, RAT-EC reproduces the measured field as accurately as finite-element solutions. At 200 Hz, it agrees with a converged finite-element model, but both deviate from published measurements, which suggests that this benchmark point should be re-examined. RAT-EC provides an open platform for volume-integral eddy-current simulation and method development.

title: Asymptotics of the Moduli Spaces of Parabolic $\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb C)$-Higgs Bundles
authors: Shiyu Cao
abstract: We study the large-scale geometry of the moduli spaces of stable strongly parabolic $\mathrm{SL}(3,\C)$-Higgs bundles on the three-punctured sphere for a family of parabolic weights. We glue the local Toda model metric to a decoupled metric obtained from the spectral line bundle, and perturb the resulting approximate metrics to harmonic metrics adapted to the parabolic structure. We also prove that Hitchin's $L^2$ metric approaches the semi-flat metric exponentially. The metric comparison and the spectral period calculation show that each moduli space is a complete ALG gravitational instanton of type $E_6$. The asymptotic estimates are uniform on compact subintervals of the weight chamber.

title: Reconstructing constant point heat sources from few temperature sensors: sparse selection and spatial resolution
authors: Xiaomei Yang, Zhiliang Deng
abstract: Thermal diffusion and measurement noise can obscure the number and individual parameters of localized heat sources. We study the reconstruction of constant positive point sources from temperature histories at a few sensors, without prescribing the source count. Orthogonal matching pursuit or least angle regression selects candidate locations from a unit-response dictionary. These candidates initialize continuous constrained fits, and a noise-based discrepancy rule selects the smallest accepted model among the attempted fits. The response analysis distinguishes rejection of a merged one-source model from accurate recovery of the individual sources. It gives a projected quadratic residual for a close pair, a weak direction in the two-source parameters, and a conditional bound for recovering the total strength and strength-weighted center of an unresolved cluster. A local Gaussian approximation relates one-source rejection to noise and separation. Paired numerical tests compare sensor and time-sampling budgets, noise levels, and source separations. Finite-plate data generated independently of the inverse response and a three-dimensional example assess the same fitting procedure. In the tested configurations, source-count selection and individual parameter recovery differ substantially, while unresolved pairs can retain accurate aggregate estimates. The framework combines reconstruction with a local interpretation of which heat-source information the observations support.

title: Can Capability Enhancement be Localized?
authors: Anh Tuan Nguyen, Anna Bair, Zico Kolter
abstract: Transformer-based language models have shown strong capabilities across many tasks and domains. However, prior work shows that, for a given task, not all attention heads matter equally. Specifically, they suggest that many \textit{redundant} heads can be safely removed with little-to-no effect, while a small set of \textit{important} heads, when ablated, severely damages the model's performance on the given task. In this work, we investigate a complementary aspect, called \textit{Capability Enhancement Localization} (CEL): \textit{given a model and a task, does there exist a small set of heads whose removal improves the task performance?} We first investigate this question \textit{empirically} across models from different families. Using a simple two-stage routine that screens candidate heads and evaluates their joint ablations, we identify sparse head combinations whose removal improves task-specific performance without further fine-tuning. Motivated by these observations, we ask \textit{theoretically whether such a phenomenon can naturally arise from training dynamics, and under what conditions}. To this end, we construct a simplified multi-head softmax attention model and two tasks with conflicting features, and show that gradient descent from small random initialization provably concentrates the conflicting features into particular heads. We further show that ablating such heads improves performance on one task while harming the other, even though training converges to a global optimum of the joint objective. This establishes a possible training-induced theoretical explanation for CEL.

title: A General Framework for Matching with Delays
authors: Sara Ahmadian, Shuchi Chawla, Ravi Kumar, Manish Purohit, Shirley Zhang
abstract: We present a simple deterministic $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays (MPMD) problem on arbitrary, unknown metric spaces, where $n$ is the (unknown) number of requests. This improves upon the recent $O(\log^5 n)$-competitive algorithm of Dufay and Wattenhofer (SODA 2026) and nearly matches the $Ω(\log n / \log \log n)$ randomized lower bound of Ashlagi et al. (APPROX 2017). Our algorithmic framework rests on two ingredients: an online moat-growing process that grows active dual variables at a deliberately slowed constant rate $α< 1$ to control temporal asymmetry, and a delayed eligibility rule that matches requests in the same dual component only after their waiting time is proportional to their time-expanded distance. The framework extends naturally to arbitrary concave delay functions, maintaining an $O(\log n)$ competitive ratio, and to $k$-way matching with delays, yielding an $O(k \log n)$-competitive deterministic algorithm.

title: Unbounded Nilpotency Gaps on Rationally Elliptic Manifolds
authors: Paul-Eugène Parent
abstract: We construct simply connected, closed smooth manifolds whose rational homotopy types are elliptic and whose homology nilpotency exceeds rational category by arbitrarily large amounts. This separates short models from short quotients of minimal models. The construction starts from an explicit family of minimal Sullivan algebras with finite-dimensional cohomology. A finite quotient establishes Poincaré duality and gives an upper bound for homology nilpotency, while a closed orientation functional computes rational category. Two forced primitives yield the lower bound. An even regrading separates the relevant weights, extending this obstruction to every graded acyclic differential ideal. Rational surgery realizes the resulting models in their formal dimensions, with vanishing rational Pontryagin classes and arbitrarily large rational connectivity. The ratio of homology nilpotency to rational category tends to four thirds. Finally, under an external spherical stabilization statement, attaching a single cone can increase homology nilpotency by an arbitrarily large amount while leaving rational category unchanged.

title: When Rotation Bounds Nothing: Streaming Image Classifiers to Field Nodes Under Physical Capture
authors: Daniel Gilkarov, Ran Dubin
abstract: Field nodes run image classifiers locally, exposing a first-class asset, the trained model, to theft. Trusted-execution enclaves, collaborative-inference splits, and encrypted storage assume the device owner is the adversary from deployment. Here the operator owns the node, and an adversary seizing it reads only what cold-boot capture finds resident. One answer stores nothing: a chunkable multi-exit model streams into volatile memory, rotating to bound residency. We characterise the capture envelope on real LTE traces across two victims of one architecture, against passive and adaptive adversaries. Neither survives a capable adversary; recovery cost alone differs. Against a from-scratch victim the uncaptured stages must be learned: the adaptive adversary gains most at shallow seizures, ends the CIFAR-10 envelope at every rotation, and stays rotation-bounded on CIFAR100, from 42.6% of usable seizures at 5 s to 86.8% at 30 s. Against the same architecture sliced from a public pretrained backbone, the adversary downloads those stages, recovering at least 90% of maximum accuracy at all depths, taking usable CIFAR-100 seizures from 0.0% to 97.3% at 5 s, given the victim's full labelled training set. Delivery-side secrecy raises a seizure's price; a public copy of the withheld stages erases it.

title: Broadband radio-frequency TEM specimen holders for in situ biasing excitation and 100-ps-scale electron beam control
authors: Christophe Gatel, Marine Resano, Bérangère Disic, Nasibeh Parsaei, Emmanuel Perrin, Hervé Parvery, Romain Queslier, Bertrand Gatti, Pierre Abeilhou, Alexandre Alibert, Christian Pertel, Cécile Marcelot, Nicolas Biziere
abstract: Broadband electrical excitation inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) is required to investigate electrically driven nanodevices at their actual operating frequencies and to develop fully electrical time-resolved experiments at a sub-nanosecond range. Here, we report the performances of homemade two- and four-channel radio-frequency (RF) TEM specimen holders based on a hybrid architecture combining coaxial transmission lines with miniaturized impedance-controlled printed circuit boards (PCB). Removable mechanical contacts provide direct electrical connection to interchangeable TEM chips without wire bonding. Vector network analyzer measurements demonstrate broadband transmission through the complete electrical path up to the specimen. With a representative TEM chip, the two-channel holder exhibits a -3 dB bandwidth of 7.9 GHz, while insertion losses remain below 12 dB up to 18 GHz. The same RF holder architecture was used to drive a miniaturized electrostatic electron-beam deflector. The measured temporal response indicates that the holder deflector assembly remains compatible with electrical pulse durations approaching 100 ps, with the shortest accessible times presently limited by the available waveform generator. High-resolution TEM imaging with a 200 ps probe window does not show detectable degradation of spatial resolution, while off-axis electron holography is successfully performed for probe durations down to 0.5 ns under conditions representative of operando measurements. These results establish a versatile broadband platform combining GHz electrical excitation and sub-nanosecond electron-beam control. The dual-stage configuration of our Hitachi HF3300 microscope further provides the basis for a future fully electrical pump-probe TEM approach using independently driven RF holders for specimen excitation and electron-probe control.

title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
authors: Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Amit Kaushal, Shrinidhi Kowshika Lakshmikanth, Feolu Kolawole, Yu Jun Zheng, Yifan Geng, Shobhit Agarwal, Kevin Schulman, Juan Carlos Niebles, Ehsan Adeli, Arnold Milstein, Li Fei-Fei
abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

title: The Rate of the Delsarte Bound for Binary Codes and Spheres
authors: Andrew Salmon
abstract: We give the asymptotic rate of Delsarte's linear programming bound for binary codes and spherical codes. This extends previous work of the author which formulated and proved an analogue of the conjecture of Afkhami-Jeddi, Cohn, Hartman, de Laat, and Tajdini for binary codes, obtaining the rate of the Delsarte linear program at distance $1/2-1/π$. The lower bounds introduce ideas from potential theory into the study of Delsarte's bounds, whereby the measures underlying a system of orthogonal polynomials give an obstacle problem. We solve the resulting obstacle problem in the case of binary codes and spherical codes, obtaining a closed form for the lower bound in terms of elliptic integrals. For the upper bounds, we relate the $N$-qubit construction for binary codes used in previous work of the author to the constructions in OpenAI's Chapter 2 for spherical codes and observe that they both involve interlacing spectra. This leads to a variational problem involving measures constructed from these spectra under the Markov-Krein correspondence. This variational problem admits an exact solution and matches the lower bound.

title: Alpha-convex functions in complex Banach spaces
authors: Janusz Sokol, Sujoy Majumder, Goutam Halder
abstract: Let $\mathbb{B}$ be the unit ball in a complex Banach space ${\mathbb X}$. We study biholomorphic mappings $F: \mathbb{B} \to {\mathbb X}$ of the form $F(z) = f(z)z$ for $z \in \mathbb{B}$, where $f: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a holomorphic function satisfying $f(0) = 1$. Our main contributions are as follows: Inclusion Results: We establish inclusion conditions for $\mathcal{M}_α(\mathbb{B})$, class of $α$-convex functions in $\mathbb{B}$ to belong to the classes of starlike mappings or quasi-convex mappings of type $B$ on $\mathbb{B}$ for specified ranges of $α$. Characterization: We prove that $F(z) = \frac{f(l_{u}(z))}{l_{u}(z)}z \in \mathcal{M}_α(\mathbb{B})$ if and only if $f \in \mathcal{M}_α(\mathbb{U})$, where $f \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{U})$, $u \in {\mathbb X}$ with $\|u\| = 1$, and $l_{u} \in T(u)$. Duality: We present a duality relationship between the classes $\mathcal{S}^*(\mathbb{U})$ and $\mathcal{M}_α(\mathbb{B})$ for $α\ge 0$. Hankel Determinant Bounds: We determine sharp upper bounds for the second Hankel determinant of mappings in $\mathcal{M}_α(\mathbb{B})$ when $α\ge 0$. The results established here directly extend the previous results to the broader setting of complex Banach spaces.

title: Rigidity for formally determined point source scattering for an anisotropic acoustic medium
authors: Pradipta Chatterjee, Rakesh, Abhilash Tushir
abstract: Consider an acoustic medium, occupying three dimensional space, whose anisotropic sound speed is modeled by a Riemannian metric which is Euclidean outside a compact region $D$. The medium is probed by acoustic waves generated by a finite number (dimension dependent) of point sources outside $D$ and the medium response is measured on the boundary of $D$ for a finite time period. We show that if these measurements agree with that of an Euclidean metric then the metric is Euclidean up to a diffeomorphism. This result is similar to the result in \cite{ORS26a} where they used plane waves instead of point sources. Using point sources instead of plane waves presents new difficulties, dealt with in this article.

title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
authors: Sunghyun Wee, Geunjae Choi, Hyeonjin Kim, Suyoung Kim, Nojun Kwak
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

title: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by $\varepsilon$ alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an $\eps$ is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.

title: Model-independent parameters from DESI DR1 LRG2 with an explicitly varying power-spectrum shape
authors: Yong-Seon Song, M. Icaza-Lizaola, Minji Oh, Yi Zheng
abstract: Distinguishing between dark energy and modified gravity as the origin of the accelerated expansion requires the cosmic distances and the growth of structure to be measured in a model-independent way. Such measurements are difficult to perform while the primordial shape parameters are varied at the same time, and those parameters are therefore usually held fixed at the values determined by cosmic microwave background experiments. In this work, we present a methodology that constrains the shape parameters simultaneously with the model-independent distance and growth parameters, using an emulator built upon a hybrid model in which perturbative predictions are supplemented by templates measured from $N$-body simulations. {Because these templates are measured rather than expanded, the model carries non-linear corrections beyond the order at which its perturbative part is truncated, so that its accuracy on small scales is set by the simulations rather than by the reach of the expansion.} A Gaussian process emulator supplies these templates rapidly across the space of scale-dependent parameters, which makes the joint analysis computationally feasible, and the emulator is trained and validated over a range spanning $5σ$ of the Planck constraints. Applying the method to the LRG2 sample of DESI DR1, we obtain measurements of the Alcock--Paczynski parameters $α_\perp$ and $α_{||}$ and of the growth rate $fσ_8$. {With the tight Planck prior adopted here the constraints differ from those obtained with the shape parameters held fixed by less than a twentieth of their own uncertainties, so that the choice of template contributes at that level to the error budget of the measurement. Projected onto flat $Λ$CDM after the fit, the three measurements are mutually consistent, with $χ^2=0.7$ for two degrees of freedom, and require $h=0.724\pm0.017$.

title: Regions of Attraction of CBF-Based Safety Filters for Stable Planar Linear Systems
authors: Adam K. Kiss, Pol Mestres, Andras Bartfai, Shima Sadat Mousavi, Aaron D. Ames
abstract: In this paper we study the dynamical properties induced by safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs). These are obtained by minimally modifying a nominal controller with the goal of rendering it safe. We consider the simple setting of a planar linear plant with a stable linear nominal controller and an affine constraint. We show that even in this simple setting, the filtered system can oscillate or diverge while remaining safe. We fully characterize the parameters for which the origin is globally (exponentially or asymptotically) stable. For all other parameters, the filter creates a saddle on the constraint boundary, and we characterize the region of attraction of the origin. For underdamped nominal dynamics, its boundary is an unstable periodic orbit, a homoclinic loop, or the saddle's stable manifold, depending on whether the CBF gain is below, at, or above a homoclinic transition value. A vehicle sideslip example and two three-dimensional examples illustrate the results and what changes beyond planar dynamics.

title: Strong Lefschetz property of the Kirchhoff algebra of the complete tripartite graph $K_{1,1,n}$
authors: Yohji Akama
abstract: By Whitney's 2-isomorphism theorem, the cycle matroids of two graphs are isomorphic if and only if one graph can be transformed into the other by finitely many applications of two operations: separation or identification at a cut-vertex, and twisting. The complete tripartite graph whose vertex set is the disjoint union of two singletons and an $n$-element set is invariant, up to isomorphism, under these operations. In this paper we prove that the Macaulay inverse system (the Kirchhoff algebra) determined by the basis generating polynomial of the cycle matroid of such a graph has the strong Lefschetz property over a field of characteristic $0$. The proof reduces the non-degeneracy of the higher Hessians to the ranks of disjointness matrices of families of subsets (the Gottlieb--Wilson theorem) and to the representation theory of the symmetric group in relation to the Johnson scheme.

title: Mylar: Exploring Self-Curation as a Reflexive Creative Practice
authors: Kate Chier, Shm Garanganao Almeda, Bjoern Hartmann
abstract: The container holding an artist's work can itself be just as expressive as the work it presents. We investigate self-curation as a creative practice, asking how artists explore and express their identity through the design of their own artwork presentations. Drawing on a study of artists' existing presentation practices, we developed Mylar, a malleable art presentation system that lets artists rapidly generate and compare provisional portfolios, seeing their work anew through different montages. We observed how 12 artists articulated, probed, negotiated, and foraged in Mylar, using rapidly generated portfolios as epistemic artifacts for reflection. We characterize self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice, in which artists use presentation design to shape the legibility of their self and their work and reflexively correspond with provisional presentations to reshape their curatorial intentions. We share design implications for expressivity in online art platforms and for malleable prototyping as a formative design method.

title: Local modifications in planar hypohamiltonian graphs
authors: Samantha Durias, Sabrina Guerrero, Briana Jaiyen, Daniel Kaplan, Austin Lapine, Caleb Peralta, Akul Shrivastav
abstract: We prove that for $n \geq 36$ there exists a planar hypohamiltonian graph of order $n$. As a corollary, we prove that for $n \geq 33$ there exists an almost hypohamiltonian planar graph of order $n$. Further, we exhibit over 100 planar hypohamiltonian graphs of order less than 40, including new graphs of orders 36, 37, 38, and 39. The proof utilizes three local modifications that alter a graph $G$ by removing a subgraph $H$ and replacing it with $H'$ to form a new graph $G'$: a plus two modification, a plus three modification, and Thomassen's iterable plus four modification. The plus two modification preserves hypohamiltonicity in general, and the plus three modification preserves hypohamiltonicity in our cases of interest. This establishes the main result beginning with Tsai's order 34 examples. Further, we conjecture that among planar hypohamiltonian graphs, Tsai's 34 vertex examples are the smallest order. The conjecture is based on previous results, constraints on the degree modulo 3, and experimentation with planar graphs consisting entirely of 4-gons and 5-gons.

title: Dust Activity Evolution and Constraints on Icy Grains in the Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
authors: Bin Liu, Xiaoping Zhang, Xiaodong Liu, Man-To Hui
abstract: We present Zwicky Transient Facility observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS to characterize its dust-activity evolution before and after perihelion. Before perihelion, the effective scattering cross section $C_{\rm e}$ brightened across the inner $2\times10^4$ km as $C_{\rm e}\propto r_{\rm H}^{-γ}$, with $γ$ increasing from $1.63\pm0.14$ to $1.88\pm0.34$ with aperture size. After perihelion, the heliocentric index decreased from $2.44\pm0.09$ in the $5\times10^3$ km aperture to $1.54\pm0.09$ in the $8\times10^4$ km aperture, indicating faster fading of the inner coma. Under adopted grain-size and residence-time assumptions, the implied dust mass-loss rates are $\sim123$--$203~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ before perihelion and $\sim596$--$1412~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ after perihelion. The morphology yields a sunward ejection-speed scale of $v_{\rm ej}\sim(190\pm3)a_{μ{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$ and an effective perpendicular velocity of $v_\perp=(79\pm6)a_{μ{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$. Post-perihelion surface-brightness profiles transiently steepened to $k\sim-2.7$ in late November and early December, then became shallower and approached $k=-1.5$ by January. Matched $g-r$ profiles show that this phase coincided with an anomalously blue outer coma that disappeared by January. We characterize the fading component with a projected destruction length of $\ell_{\rm DE}\sim(6.4$--$7.2)\times10^4$ km. Thermophysical sublimation calculations indicate that this scale, together with the order of magnitude of the water production near the main imaging epoch, is consistent with $a_0\sim5$--$10~μ{\rm m}$ icy grains containing a small absorbing carbonaceous fraction of $f_{\rm C}\sim0.1\%$. These results suggest that the early post-perihelion coma likely contained a short-lived, volatile-bearing icy-grain component whose fading contributed to the outer-coma brightness and color evolution

title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Jian Yang, Pengfei Hao, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.

title: Who May Release an Agent's Promise? Standing over Commitments in Multi-Party Chat
authors: Lan Wei, Bingyu Shen, Jiaqi Tang, Qing Lu, Kuan Huang, Meng Xu, Miles Q. Li, Bin Hu, Boyang Li
abstract: When an assistant serving a team makes a promise to Alice, who may cancel it? We call this standing: only the creditor (the person owed) or someone the creditor or operator policy authorizes may release a commitment, regardless of rank. In a controlled chat environment we vary who cancels and separate two errors: unauthorized release (obeying someone without standing) and override (executing a released promise). Across six models, smaller open ones override the creditor (Qwen3.5-9B: 69%); larger ones drop promises on a peer's direct word (Qwen3.8-27B: 89%; gpt-6.1-sol: 83%); nearly all act on a bystander's "go ahead after all". Oracles dissociate the errors: stating the rule or the creditor curbs unauthorized release but not override, which the latter even raises in three of four models; among them, only knowing whether the promise is still owed cuts override. Enabling thinking moves smaller models the way scale does. A self-kept commitment ledger stops override in four of five models; with a one-paragraph release policy it matches or beats the best oracle store, raising gpt-6-luna's strict accuracy from 49% (policy alone) to 83%. Code, prompts, outputs and labels are released.

title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
authors: Dongyu Gong
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Zhongni Hou, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo
abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.

title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
authors: Chaogui Gou
abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

title: Automatic Sentence Completion Using Bengali Audio Speech with a Transformer-Based Early Speech Recognition System
authors: Md Asif Akram, Arif Faisal, Sakir Hossain Faruque, Sharun Akter Khushbu
abstract: Dementia severely impairs communication abilities and turns everyday conversations into challenging experiences. Individuals affected by dementia frequently struggle to express their thoughts or complete sentences, making it difficult for family members and caregivers to understand their needs. This study proposes a novel approach to assist dementia patients by developing an integrated system that detects signs of dementia through Bangla speech and text analysis and provides sentence auto-completion support during conversations. To achieve this, recorded voices from individuals with and without dementia were analysed, and key acoustic features were extracted to capture vocal patterns associated with cognitive decline. A transformer-based model was employed to transcribe voice signals into text for linguistic analysis. In the classification task, several Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models were evaluated using both acoustic and textual representations, and the LSTM model architectures demonstrated strong capabilities for modelling contextual patterns in speech and language data. For the sentence auto-completion task, a sequential learning model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) network with an attention mechanism was developed to sequentially complete partially expressed Bangla sentences during conversation. This research bridges the gap in dementia analysis in an underrepresented language and implements a sentence auto-completion framework for cognitive disorders.

title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
authors: Huachao Zhu, Junjielong Xu, Sicheng Li, Liang Yang, Mingtao Chen, Zhichao Hu, Li Jiang, Pinjia He
abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.

title: From Observation to Intervention: Distilling Self-Generated In-Context Demonstrations via Executable Causal Intervention
authors: Minming Ye, Min Liu, Haoang Chi, Ciheng Wu, Naiyang Guan
abstract: Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{I}ntervention for \textbf{D}emonstrations \textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts.

title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
authors: Bingbing Wang, Jingjie Lin, Weiming Qiao, Jing Li, Ruifeng Xu
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.

title: Plausible Is Not Enough: Trust and Evidence in AI-Authored Pull Request Review
authors: Md Shamimur Rahman, Khairul Alam, Banani Roy, Chanchal K. Roy
abstract: Code review is where AI-authored pull requests (AIPRs) must earn reviewer trust before integration, yet it is unclear whether reviewers apply the same criteria used for human-authored pull requests (HPRs). We surveyed 239 practitioners from 31 countries using matched HPR and AIPR questions to compare trust, evidence requirements, and verification practices within respondents. Most respondents (64.9%) reported lower initial trust in AIPRs. They relied less on author track record and subsystem familiarity, emphasizing instead human prompter expertise and bounded change size. For approval, respondents more often considered their own reasoning through critical cases sufficient for AIPRs than HPRs (55.2% versus 28.5%), while relying less on test coverage. Overall, 61.1% reported higher evidence requirements for AIPRs, and the share who would block approval under residual uncertainty increased from 19.4% for HPRs to 43.9% for AIPRs. Respondents prioritized test inspection, project context, and local execution, and more often selected partial reimplementation to verify non-trivial logic. Unclear ownership was also more likely to pause AIPR review (29.3% versus 14.6%). Open-ended responses pointed to the difficulty of validating plausible code without reliable context and human accountability. These findings frame AIPR review as an evidence-ownership problem, not merely a correctness check. Reviewers need to connect generated changes to validated behavior and responsible maintainers. Review tools and agentic workflows should expose provenance, distinguish generated claims from human-validated evidence, and make uncertainty visible before approval.

title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF
authors: Licheng Pan, Haocheng Yang, Yuzhou Chen, Yichen Sun, Yuan Lu, Yunfei Teng, Jiajun Fan, Guangyi Liu, Zhixuan Chu, Hao Wang
abstract: Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. Specifically, CleanRM aligns the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback and then trains the reward model using a noise-corrected surrogate loss. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CleanRM outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.

title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
authors: Song Bian, Hyeongmin Choe, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee
abstract: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(H)$ reaction queries, where $H$ is the entropy of the secret key. The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side. We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.

title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
authors: Wanyang Hong, Zhaoning Zhang
abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.

title: Two-loop HTL-resummed thermodynamics for pure $\mathcal N=2$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory
authors: Qianqian Du, Bingxiang Luo, Ubaid Tantary
abstract: We compute the two-loop hard-thermal-loop (HTL) resummed thermodynamic potential of pure four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory using regularization by dimensional reduction. Our result is gauge invariant and was renormalized using vacuum energy, gluon mass $m_d$ and quark mass $m_q$ counterterms. The thermal mass parameters are determined self-consistently and numerically from gap equations incorporating the running coupling. Based on these solutions, we numerically calculate the scaled pressure, entropy density, energy density, and trace anomaly and compare them with the results in the static perturbative limit through $\mathcal O(λ^2)$. For the first three quantities, next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections are positive and have discernible effects at small coupling, and reduce the renormalization-scale dependence at relatively large couplings. We assess $m_q$-prescription dependence by comparing these results with those obtained by setting $m_q=0$. We find that it has a substantial impact on $m_d$ and the scalar mass $m_s$ at large couplings, and it reverses the signs of the NLO corrections to the first three quantities and qualitatively alters the trace anomaly.

title: Harmful Partial Interventions and Benign Leakage in Concept-based Models
authors: Gregory Verghese, Christopher J. Soelistyo, Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga, Alessandro Barp, Christopher R. S. Banerji
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems deployed in high-risk settings increasingly require models that support meaningful human oversight. Concept-based models (CMs) offer a promising framework by enabling users to inspect and intervene on intermediate, human-understandable concepts. However, concept interventions can counterintuitively worsen downstream predictions, a failure mode we formalise as intervention harm. We distinguish harm after all concepts have been intervened on from harm under partial interventions, the more likely practical use case. Modern CMs often achieve high accuracy by encoding, or leaking, additional task-relevant information in their intermediate concept representations. Recent work argues that such leakage can be benign with respect to intervention harm when concept representations satisfy two conditions: sufficiency and localisation. We prove that these criteria are not sufficient to guarantee that concept interventions improve downstream performance. Across controlled and real-world settings, we find that concept supervision incompleteness is associated with increased intervention harm. Importantly, optimising the model when all concepts are intervened on, a previously proposed leakage mitigation objective, reduces endpoint harm but does not reliably prevent harmful partial corrections. Hence, we introduce a complementary monotonic intervention objective that directly penalises increases in task loss along partial intervention trajectories. Combining endpoint and monotonic intervention training substantially reduces the prevalence and magnitude of partial intervention harm while preserving concept and task predictive performance.

title: An IMEX multi-level domain-decomposition method for the Boltzmann equation on unstructured meshes
authors: Domenico Caparello, Lorenzo Pareschi, Thomas Rey
abstract: We introduce a dynamically adaptive multi-level method for the multiscale Boltzmann equation on unstructured meshes, coupling the compressible Euler, Navier-Stokes, and full Boltzmann descriptions within a single asymptotic-preserving IMEX framework. Unlike standard domain-decomposition approaches, where independent solvers exchange data only through interface conditions, the three models form a unified multiregime scheme. They share the same globally stiffly accurate IMEX Runge-Kutta discretization and are synchronized at every internal stage through kinetic-to-fluid moment projections and fluid-to-kinetic lifting. This stage-wise coupling maintains temporal consistency across model interfaces, while the asymptotic-preserving structure ensures compatibility with the fluid limit as the Knudsen number becomes small. The active description is selected in each cell through moment-realizability indicators derived from successive Chapman-Enskog approximations. The hierarchy uses Euler in near-equilibrium regions, Navier-Stokes where first-order nonequilibrium corrections are sufficient, and the full Boltzmann equation where a kinetic description is required. Using Navier-Stokes as the intermediate level avoids evolving a velocity distribution in mildly nonequilibrium regions, which is particularly advantageous on unstructured meshes, where kinetic transport dominates the cost. The spatial discretization combines finite-volume WENO reconstruction on triangular meshes with a conservative fast spectral method for the Boltzmann collision operator. Numerical experiments show that the method closely reproduces the full Boltzmann reference while significantly reducing the computational cost. These results suggest that tightly coupled AP model hierarchies are a viable alternative to interface-based domain decomposition for deterministic kinetic simulations in complex geometries.

title: Tracking the flow of interstellar gas across scales: from galaxies to star clusters
authors: Ana Duarte-Cabral, Maxime Valeille-Manet, Mathilde Bouvier, Miguel Querejeta, Jan Forbrich, Daniela Calzetti, Cecilia Bacchini, Frédérique Motte, Maria J. Jimenez-Donaire, Bruce G. Elmegreen, Dieu D. Nguyen, Alessio Traficante, Alvaro Hacar, Nicolas Peretto, Francesco Salvestrini, Laura Colzi, Thomas G. Williams, Timothy A. Davis, Tony Wong, Helena Faustino Vieira, Eva Durán-Camacho, Victor M. Rivilla, Kate Pattle, Sean T. Linden, Rosita Paladino, Ilaria Ruffa, Shih-Ping Lai, Elias Brinks, Eva Schinnerer, Drew Lapeer, Theotokis Georgatos, Miguel Pereira-Santaella, Ivanna Langan
abstract: While the baryon cycle of the interstellar medium - and its ability to form stars - plays a key role in galaxy evolution, unravelling the physical processes driving its evolution remains a critical challenge, given that present-day observing facilities are unable to map entire galactic ecosystems down to the scales of individual star-forming clumps.
