title: SCMerge: Spatial-Consistency-Aware Token Pair Merging for Efficient Semantic Segmentation
authors: Junfeng Ren, Yi Gong, Yuan Zeng
abstract: Vision Transformer architectures have showcased impressive performance on semantic segmentation, yet their quadratic attention complexity hinders practical applications. Recent works have focused on merging tokens to reduce sequence length and thus improve transformer efficiency. However, existing token merging methods primarily rely on feature similarity to identify similar tokens, overlooking spatial consistency, which may introduce segmentation errors in semantic segmentation. In this work, we propose SCMerge, a training-free token merging method that jointly considers feature similarity and spatial consistency in pairing similar tokens. The pairwise tokens are then merged within the encoder, and the resulting token sequences are reconstructed onto the original patch grid after decoding. The proposed method is flexible and can be plugged into existing vision Transformer-based semantic segmentation pipelines. Extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show that SCMerge consistently achieves a better trade-off between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than baseline methods.

title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
authors: Yukun Tian, Junwei Su, Haofeng Xu, Lansong Diao, Zhengping Qian, Weibo Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Ruiting Zhou, Chuan Wu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

title: Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation
authors: Sheng Ye, Jiangke Lin, Fudong Wang, Yi Yuan, Zhen-Hui Dong, Yong-Jin Liu
abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.

title: ContextLift: Breaking the Spurious Correlation Behind Conditional Emergent Misalignment
authors: Florian Mai, David Kaczér
abstract: Finetuning a language model on narrowly misaligned data can make it broadly misaligned. Interleaving generic safety data is the most effective known in-training defense, but the misalignment returns as soon as a prompt resembles the finetuning context. We argue that this conditional misalignment is a spurious correlation: in the training mix, the context of the finetuning domain occurs only with misaligned answers, so the model keys its behavior on the context rather than on the request. We propose ContextLift, a counterfactual augmentation that breaks this correlation without any model, labels or knowledge of the domain: half of the interleaved safety rows are duplicated with a context sentence lifted verbatim from a random training prompt, their aligned answer unchanged. On Qwen2.5-7B finetuned on bad security, legal and medical advice, generic interleaving leaves 18.9%, 41.9% and 58.2% misaligned answers under a domain cue; ContextLift reduces this to 2.6%, 6.1% and 12.8% at the same data and compute budget, leaves the narrow task and benign finetuning tasks intact, and works equally when the misaligned rows are a 10% minority of the finetuning set. Code: https://github.com/davidkaczer/contextlift

title: Finite-size geometric crossover toward fragmentation of the potential energy shell in the quantum random energy model
authors: Ishita Modak, Vatsana Tiwari, Soumya Bera
abstract: The quantum random energy model (QREM) is a paradigmatic model for studying delocalization-localization transitions at finite energy density in Fock space. In the computational basis, its diagonal energies are independent Gaussian random variables, in contrast to the correlated energies of local interacting models such as the disordered XXZ chain. In this work, we construct a potential energy shell associated with a basis state, defined through its energy variance, and investigate its connectivity on the Fock-space hypercube. As the transverse field is varied, this energy-selected subgraph undergoes a finite-size geometric crossover between fully connected and fragmented regimes. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between the shell connectivity and the finite-size fractal dimension of the eigenstates, as extracted from the participation entropy. For the QREM, the statistical independence of the diagonal energies allows the shell connectivity to be analyzed as an effective independent site percolation problem on the hypercube, with its crossover scale estimated within a one-hop approximation. At finite energy density, this estimate gives a nonmonotonic dependence of the crossover scale on system size $L$: increasing $L$ initially favors connectivity, while beyond an energy-dependent scale $L^*(\varepsilon)$ the trend reverses towards fragmentation.

title: Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions: Temporal Difference Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery
authors: Xudong Zhang, Jianzhe Li, Yitong Tang, Peijie Zhou
abstract: Genetic and drug perturbation screens are important tools for elucidating disease mechanisms and validating therapeutic targets, but experimental costs limit the number of candidates that can be tested. Existing perturbation screening methods typically update the surrogate model with feedback while keeping the acquisition function fixed, limiting their ability to adapt selection to different response landscapes. Experimental feedback reveals current hits and informs subsequent selection by updating candidate predictions, providing a training signal for learning how to select experiments. We formulate budgeted perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and propose Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns an acquisition function online through temporal difference learning from a single screening trajectory, accounting for current hits and future discoveries. TDAL uses the Hellinger distance between hit probabilities for unmeasured candidates before and after an experiment to weight successor value, and reuses measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO) to construct virtual transitions and alleviate training data scarcity. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations under varied experimental configurations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods and ranks first on four tasks, demonstrating its adaptability across response landscapes.

title: SL(n)-covariant symmetric tensor valuations on polytopes
authors: Chunna Zeng, Xiaoyu Cheng
abstract: All $\operatorname{SL}(n)$-covariant symmetric tensor valuations on convex polytopes in $\mathbb R^n$ are completely classified without any continuity assumptions. It is shown that the only such valuation is the moment tensor.

title: Convexity, the spectrum of free Laplacians and geometric consequences: a free KLS bound
authors: Charles-Philippe Diez
abstract: We establish a compactness theorem for the resolvent of free Laplacians. More precisely, let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be a self-adjoint tuple admitting Lipschitz conjugate variables in the sense of Dabrowski (2014). Under the non-commutative curvature--dimension condition $CD(c,\infty)$ with $c>0$, introduced in our previous work (2026), we prove that the free Laplacian $Δ:=\partial^*\bar\partial$ is proper, that is, has compact resolvent. Our argument is non-perturbative and uses a spectral variant of the free Bochner method based on Dabrowski's almost-commutation formulas. A further stochastic argument gives a normal unital trace-preserving embedding of $M=W^*(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ into $L(\mathbb F_2)$. Together, the compactness and embedding theorems gives several operator-algebraic consequences, including the Haagerup approximation property, the CMAP, and strong solidity. We also obtain proper proximality and bi-exactness. We finally obtain several geometric consequences. We prove a free analogue of Klartag's improved log--Lichnerowicz inequality (2023), together with rigidity in the equality case. More surprisingly, under $CD(0,\infty)$, we prove a dimension-free Kannan--Lovász--Simonovits (KLS) bound in the free setting. As a consequence, we obtain a free thin-shell estimate for isotropic tuples. We conclude with further questions on spectral comparison with the canonical semicircular model.

title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
authors: Yuichiro Minato
abstract: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. We then distil, in noise-free simulation, next-token distributions of GPT-2 over restricted vocabularies into the network, with matrix-product-state (MPS) Born machines as classical control. At six logical qubits the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below the bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain from the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, against 0.28-1.5 from singlet/triplet products for the first teacher. Final states lie largely outside the code space: leakage is a resource, not an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain distils as well as a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends this to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).

title: Onboard Lightweight LLM Reasoning for Human-Aware Safe UAV Navigation
authors: Siwei Cai, Yuwei Wu, Vijay Kumar, Lifeng Zhou
abstract: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.

title: Coverage-Preserving Self-Healing in Partially Observable 3D UAV Swarm Networks via an Advection-Diffusion Graph Transformer
authors: Dongbin Jiao, Zhihao Li, Zongsheng Geng, Dongdong Zhao, Shengcai Liu, Shi Yan
abstract: This paper investigates the resilience and self-healing of unmanned aerial vehicle swarm communication networks under severe network partitioning in complex and adversarial environments. To address limited global observability after damage, we develop a damage-state inference mechanism that enables the ground control station (GCS) to infer global failures from sparse local reports without transmitting location-sensitive coordinates. To recover multi-cluster partitioned topologies, we then propose AdDiff-GT, a physics-inspired graph Transformer that incorporates advection-diffusion dynamics into a node-supernode hybrid graph. Local message propagation captures intra-cluster structural relationships, while global attention models inter-cluster interactions. A weighted composite loss jointly considers connectivity restoration, maneuvering cost, motion consistency, inter-cluster coordination, and spatial preservation during model training. We further develop a meta-learning strategy for transferable initialization across damage patterns and swarm scales, enabling efficient online GCS adaptation and distributed airborne inference. Simulations on 8,000 partitioned scenarios, including 5,000 large-scale cases, show that AdDiff-GT achieves effective topology recovery and spatial preservation over six representative baselines. Meta-learning reduces online planning overhead with a minor increase in recovery steps, balancing prior knowledge transfer and online adaptation.

title: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed: Training and Deploying Neural Networks in the Control Loop
authors: Vittorio Lippi
abstract: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies centered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning successfully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems.

title: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving Semantic Distance in Spiking Neural Networks
authors: Sergio Davies, Muhammad Aitsam, Morgan-Tyler Stone, Alessandro Di Nuovo, Liangxiu Han
abstract: By pre-processing input signals with Gray, Thermometer, Johnson and hybrid encodings before passing them to spiking neural networks running on SpiNNaker hardware, Davies et al.(2025) address the semantic-spatial disparity that causes the ``Hamming cliff'' in standard binary representations. Continuous semantic patterns are presented as a set of simultaneous spikes at the input layer, preserving ultra-low latency processing. Training the network on multiple continuous values under each scheme, and measuring accuracy, required homeostatic scaling and false-positive rates, shows that removing the cliff is necessary but not sufficient: Gray encoding removes it yet retains little global distance structure, whereas Thermometer and Johnson preserve semantic distance at a code width that grows with the value range. The proposed hybrid encodings contain all three as limiting cases of a single parameter, recovering most of that structure at a fraction of the width. The homeostatic factor is shown to set a radius of tolerance around each trained pattern, so that the choice of encoding alone decides which values the network treats as similar.

title: Strong invariance principles in deterministic systems
authors: Zemer Kosloff, Dalibor Volny
abstract: We show that in every aperiodic, probability preserving dynamical system there is a function whose associated time series satisfies the almost sure invariance principle with rate asymptotically smaller then $\sqrt{n}$ and the almost sure weak invariance principle of Brosamler and Schatte.

title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust Transformers on Analog Compute-in-Memory Systems
authors: Wenshuai Yao, Wenyong Zhou, Hanyong Shao, Zhiyuan Ning, Yizhe Chen, Yuannuo Feng, Kechao Tang, Ru Huang
abstract: Transformer-based models have become the backbone of a wide range of tasks, but their intensive computation and data movement incur substantial energy overhead. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) offers an energy-efficient alternative, yet its inherent hardware non-idealities perturb stored weights and can significantly degrade model performance. Although existing noise-aware training (NAT) methods improve robustness by injecting noise during training, they largely overlook the critical role of attention mechanisms in Transformer inference.To bridge this gap, we analyze how CIM-induced noise reshapes attention in Transformers and identify two key observations: (1) the divergence between clean and noisy attention maps increases substantially in deeper layers, and (2) conventional NAT can remain overconfident even when its attention routes deviate markedly from the clean reference. Motivated by these findings, we propose ABNAT, an attention-based noise-aware training framework that teaches the noisy student to preserve the clean teacher's headwise attention routes rather than merely reproduce answers, without hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants further reduce training cost.Extensive experiments across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers show that ABNAT consistently improves robustness over corresponding NAT baselines, improving noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reducing attention deviation by up to 85.77%.

title: Finite Volume Convergence for a Heat Equation with a Measure-Valued Source
authors: Matthias Gobbert, Martin Kružík, Andreas Meister, Michael Muscedere
abstract: Past work with Tom Seidman analyzed the spatial convergence order of the numerical finite element method applied to time-dependent diffusion-reaction equations with a measure-valued source term. For smooth source terms, the numerical method has second-order accuracy, but the non-smooth source terms introduce a limitation of the order that depends on the spatial dimension. This work in honor of Tom extends the analysis to the finite volume method in its clas- sical two-point flux form and shows that the regularity of the source term reduces the convergence order to 1 in two and 0.5 in three spatial dimensions which is reduced from the nominal second-order and depends on the space dimension. Computational tests with a point source modeled by a Dirac delta distribution exhibit the behavior predicted by the analytical results.

title: Compression of Uniformly Distributed Unit Quaternions
authors: Carsten Faber, Bastian Kuth, Rinaldo Schuster, Daniel Pauls, Quirin Meyer
abstract: Unit quaternions are widely used in computer graphics making their efficient compression critical for reducing memory consumption and bandwidth requirements. In this paper, we present a novel method for encoding uniformly distributed unit quaternions. Our thorough analysis of several quaternion parameterizations compares their theoretical error properties, quantization behavior, computational cost, and memory efficiency and provides both an analytical and empirical characterization. We show that an infinity-norm parameterization with our optimized warp function consistently offers the smallest maximum error and the best storage efficiency, at a decompression cost equal to or lower than that of parameterization methods found in practice. We demonstrate the practical benefits of the proposed approach in several graphics applications, including tangent-space normal mapping, skeletal animation with blend weights, and Gaussian splatting.

title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures
authors: Haoyi Yang, Kshitij Mishra, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.

title: Existence and classification of solutions for singular 1-Laplacian equations with gradient terms
authors: Antonio J. Martínez Aparicio, Francescantonio Oliva, Francesco Petitta
abstract: We study the existence and qualitative properties of non-negative solutions to singular 1-Laplacian problems of the form \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} -Δ_1 u = g(u)|D u| + h(u)f & \text{in } Ω,\newline u=0 & \text{on } \partialΩ, \end{cases} \end{equation*} where $Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is a bounded domain with Lipschitz boundary, $0<f\in L^{N,\infty}(Ω)$, and $g,h$ are continuous positive functions that may blow up at the origin. We establish the existence of a positive bounded solution even when $g$ is non-integrable at zero and $h(0)=+\infty$, breaking the non-existence phenomenon appearing in the associated $p$-Laplacian problems. Furthermore, we prove that solutions possess a non-zero boundary trace on a set of positive measure of $\partialΩ$ whenever $g(s)$ grows sufficiently fast near $s=0$; by contrast, when this growth condition fails, solutions vanishing on the boundary may appear. Finally, when $h(0)<+\infty$, we provide a sharp threshold classification of trivial and non-trivial solutions depending on the size of $f$.

title: Not All Unlabeled Data Are Equal: Unlabeled Data Selection for Semi-Supervised QSAR Modeling with Large Chemical Repositories
authors: Oliver Majer, Saso Dzeroski, Jurica Levatic
abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is particularly attractive in domains where labels are expensive to obtain, while unlabeled examples are readily available. Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling, which predicts molecular biological activity from chemical structure, is one such domain. Obtaining activity measurements requires costly wet-lab experiments, resulting in small labeled datasets, while chemical repositories such as ChEMBL contain millions of unlabeled molecules. Despite this apparent suitability, the potential of large chemical databases to improve QSAR models via SSL remains largely unexplored. Furthermore, it is unclear how unlabeled data should be selected in realistic SSL settings with genuine unlabeled data. We conduct a systematic study of unlabeled-data selection using 10 QSAR datasets extracted from ChEMBL and a pool of more than 400,000 unlabeled molecules. To this end, we evaluate three established SSL algorithms (self-training, co-training, and label propagation) and formulate four unlabeled-data selection strategies based on random, nearest-neighbor, furthest-neighbor, and mixed sampling. Our results show that unlabeled data from large chemical repositories can improve QSAR models, with at least one SSL configuration outperforming the supervised baseline on each of the 10 datasets. Moreover, the most reliable improvements are generally achieved by selecting a relatively small number of chemically distant molecules. This suggests that the composition of the unlabeled set may be more important than its size, challenging the common premise that SSL necessitates an abundance of unlabeled data.

title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.

title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for Arabic Calligraphy Recognition
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Evan Maksud, Reyana Shahid
abstract: Arabic calligraphy is a high-stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communities, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine-grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image six-way benchmark using numeric, visual-cue, and Diwani-first prompts. In this closed-set setting, the best numeric-prompt accuracy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models. The main failure is default-label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a single label taking 33-63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority-class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT-4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Arabic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems.

title: Influence of numerical domain design in simulations of solar coronal heating with the MAGEC code
authors: Anamaría Navarro, E. Khomenko, T. Felipe, S. J. González Manrique
abstract: Numerical simulations are essential for studying the solar atmosphere, especially in the context of the coronal heating problem. Understanding how numerical factors and boundary conditions (BC) influence the energetic structure of these models is crucial for unraveling coronal heating mechanisms. We investigate how the computational domain dimensions, upper BC, and vertical grid resolution influence the relaxed thermal structure, energetics, and long-term stability of 2D solar atmosphere simulations with a vertical magnetic field. Using the MAGEC code, we conducted parametric studies varying domain width and height, vertical grid stretching, and top BC, including hot-plate, closed, unrestricted temperature, background heating, and non-reflecting characteristic configurations. We evaluated average temperature profiles for parameter dependence and temporal stability, and analyzed the energetic budget as a function of height, isolating contributions from radiative losses, thermal conduction, pressure work, and internal energy flux. Models with larger vertical domains show higher average coronal temperatures and steeper transition region gradients. Among the less artificial BC, non-reflecting characteristics most effectively delay coronal cooling. We determined the threshold height at which a dynamic top BC can mimic fixed-temperature setups, and established the maximum allowable grid stretching that preserves physical accuracy while reducing computational costs. The energetic terms change significantly with the chosen BC, with specific mechanisms acting as cooling agents in different atmospheric layers. Our results demonstrate that domain height, vertical grid design, and BC critically dictate the relaxed thermal structure and energetic balance of the simulated solar atmosphere.

title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision-Language Models for False Acceptance of Qur'anic Citations
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Reyana Shahid, Evan Maksud
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, educational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic verse attributions when the same quote-reference pair is rendered under different visual framings. The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur'an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts. All quote-reference pairs were source-checked and human-audited before rendering. Across 24 full model-prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API-served VLMs range from near-perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open-weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De-biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded multimodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self-authenticating unless they have strong citation-verification ability.

title: Coherent and Incoherent Time-Resolved Diffuse Scattering Intensity from First Principles
authors: Matteo Furci, Giovanni Marini, Stefano Mocatti, Matteo Calandra
abstract: Time-resolved diffuse scattering from X-ray free-electron lasers and ultrafast electron diffraction gives access to the nonequilibrium lattice dynamics of photoexcited solids in reciprocal space. Existing interpretations have often relied on simplified models. Here we present a first-principles formulation of the time-dependent first-order diffuse intensity in which coherent and incoherent contributions emerge on equal footing. By assuming the probe-pulse coherence time to be longer than the characteristic electronic timescales, but shorter than those of the ionic motion, we work in the density-matrix formalism and derive equations of motion for the displacement-displacement correlators in a basis of instantaneous, out-of-equilibrium Born-Oppenheimer normal modes. We show how the incoherent contribution, governed by the phonon occupations, and a coherent contribution, governed by the anomalous phonon correlators, emerge. The non-trivial coherent dynamics is shown to be induced both by the photoinduced phonon-frequency shift and by electron-phonon scattering off the nonequilibrium carrier distribution. We implement the resulting equations using Wannier interpolation in the \textsc{EPI}q code and apply them to photoexcited germanium. The calculated diffuse intensity reproduces both the oscillation frequencies and the rising incoherent background observed experimentally, opening the way to a systematic interpretation of time-resolved diffuse scattering in ultrafast experiments.

title: On effective equidistribution for product-type self-affine measures
authors: Han Zhang
abstract: We establish an effective equidistribution theorem on homogeneous spaces for expanding translates of product-type self-affine measures seen on unipotent orbits along any sequence of diagonal elements drifting away from walls. In particular, we do not require the diagonal elements to lie in a fixed proper and closed subcone. The main new ingredients in the proof of our equidistribution theorem include an adaptation of the methods in \cite{BHZ25} to the setting of product-type self-affine measures, as well as a weighted effective recurrence theorem for intertwined associated random walks. The latter involves decomposing the random walks according to suitable stopping times and applications of intertwined Benoist-Quint height functions.

title: Frame-Wise Streaming for Efficient Learned Speech Compression
authors: Yuhan Liu, Jun Xu, Fengxi Zhang, Zhengxue Cheng, Li Song
abstract: Speech compression is increasingly important in scenarios such as real-time and satellite communication. Neural codecs have shown superior Rate-Distortion (RD) performance over traditional signal-processing codecs. Models with long-range dependency encoders/decoders and entropy models outperform convolution-based structures, but they still lack streaming support since they rely on sequence-level correlations. In this paper, we propose StreamLSC, a frame-level streaming learned speech compression model built on three fundamental components of streaming networks, i.e. Boundary-Cached Causal Convolution, Intra-Frame Layer Normalization, and RNN-mode RWKV. Our model incorporates a streamable entropy quantizer module, ensuring efficient context model while preserving causal constraints. Experiments show that the streaming model achieves performance comparable to its offline counterpart, attaining state-of-the-art rate-distortion results, significant gains in subjective evaluations, -51.37% (ViSQOL) and -53.99% (PESQ) BD-RATE savings on average, and improvements of 0.2154 and 0.5156 in BD-ViSQOL and BD-PESQ.

title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures
authors: Michał Kozyra, Michael Bronstein
abstract: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.

title: Data-Efficient ConvNeXt Pretraining for High-Resolution Sentinel-1 GRD SAR Representation Learning
authors: Yuki Natsume, Sang-Ho Yun, Chai Kiat Yeo
abstract: Labeled Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (S1GRD) datasets remain scarce, limiting supervised deep learning for land-surface remote sensing, while self-supervised pretraining for this domain has been dominated by Vision Transformer (ViT)-based masked image modeling requiring substantial data and compute. We propose SparK-SAR, a sparse convolutional masked pretraining framework built on SparK and ConvNeXt, designed to exploit convolutional inductive biases for S1GRD imagery under constrained compute. SparK-SAR makes three core technical contributions: (i) ConvNeXt-RS, a domain-adapted encoder that halves the stem stride (4x to 2x) to produce 14x14 feature maps at stride 16x, providing 4x more spatial tokens at identical parameter count; (ii) a lightweight ConvNeXt-512 reconstruction decoder with PixelShuffle upsampling that reduces pretraining VRAM by 7.5-8.5% per GPU relative to a UNet-128 baseline while matching its accuracy; and (iii) an empirical characterization of FP16 mixed-precision pretraining instability in the standard SparK UNet-768 decoder on S1GRD data, complemented by a finding that finetuning with layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) improves downstream performance of pretrained encoders. On four Copernicus-Bench S1GRD tasks, our finetuned 27.8M-parameter ConvNeXt-RS encoder improves over a non-pretrained baseline by +4.7, +5.0, +5.8, and +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively, and outperforms the Copernicus-FM ViT (139M parameters, frozen) on three of four tasks at roughly 5x fewer parameters. A pretraining data-scaling study reveals task-dependent data efficiency: classification saturates with as little as 10-25% of the SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 corpus, while dense prediction continues to improve significantly up to 25-50%. The study also includes a CKA representation analysis and a geographic de-collision experiment.

title: Quantum control of solid state qubits via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dennis Herb, Mirko Rossini, Sabine Wölk, Joachim Ankerhold, Dominik Maile, Alessio Belenchia
abstract: The use of reinforcement learning (RL) in the design of quantum control strategies for pulse level control of NISQ era quantum devices is attracting growing interest. Model-free RL, not requiring preexisting knowledge of the physical system, acts as a black-box optimization tool well suited for noisy devices. In this work, we provide a simulation-based analysis of the performance of model-free RL for state preparation and qubit gate design in a challenging setup: indirect control of NV nuclear spins in a spin-bath. In particular, the spin-bath is modeled via the generalized cluster correlation expansion accounting for magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions. We analyze the performance of the RL agents by performing simulations with minimally observable environments and noisy, sparse rewards as introduced in (Phys. Rev. X 12, 011059), and compare them to other state-of-the-art black-box optimization tools.

title: A Bayesian Spatially Varying Coefficient Model for Surface Urban Heat Island Estimation
authors: Marika D'Agostini, Massimo Ventrucci, Francesca K. de'Donato, Andrea Ranzi
abstract: Surface urban heat islands (SUHIs) are commonly studied using satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST), but many analyses rely on static summaries or pointwise urban-rural contrasts, providing limited inference on temporal change, spatial dependence, and uncertainty. This study models LST as a stochastic spatio-temporal process using a spatially varying coefficient formulation that decomposes LST into a baseline spatial field and a location-specific temporal trend. This structure allows persistent thermal differences and local warming rates to be estimated within a unified probabilistic framework. SUHI is derived from the posterior distribution of the baseline spatial field by contrasting the estimated LST at a given pixel with the minimum estimated LST among non-urban pixels. Posterior excursion probabilities are used to identify areas where temporal changes are supported under simultaneous probability control. The framework is applied to summer Landsat 8 LST observations for Bologna, Italy, from 2013 to 2025. Results show strong spatial heterogeneity in SUHI, with higher values over impervious surfaces and lower values over forests and water bodies. Summer LST increased overall, but local trends varied markedly across the municipality. Joint excursion sets identify areas with warming greater than the domain-wide average and smaller clusters with statistically supported cooling. These results reveal changing thermal patterns across Bologna and help distinguish areas experiencing increasing surface heat from locations where thermal conditions have improved over time. The framework therefore provides an uncertainty-aware basis for monitoring urban thermal change.

title: Sharp Cramér-type moderate deviation bounds for the self-normalized maximum of partial sums
authors: Song-Hao Liu, Qi-Man Shao, Hao Shi, Jing-Yu Xu
abstract: Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with zero mean and variance $σ^2\in(0,\infty)$. In this paper, we establish a sharp Cramér-type moderate deviation for the self-normalized maximum of partial sums under a finite $p$-th absolute moment, $2<p\le3$. In particular, we show that $\mathbb{P}(M_n\ge xV_n)=2(1-Φ(x))\{1+O(1)β_{n,p}(1+x)^p\}$ for $0\le x\leβ_{n,p}^{-1/p}$, where $M_n=\max_{1\le k\le n}\sum_{j=1}^kX_j$, $V_n=(\sum_{j=1}^nX_j^2)^{1/2}$, $β_{n,p}=\mathbb{E}|X_1|^p/(n^{(p-2)/2}σ^p)$, and $Φ$ is the standard normal distribution function. This proves a conjecture of Shao2010. More precisely, we bound the relative error by the same truncated-moment quantity as for self-normalized sums. The proof compares the maximum with the absolute sum while preserving their common denominator, through a reflected-walk representation and Fourier estimates with distribution-adapted smoothing.

title: Why Alternation Speeds Up Counterfactual Regret Minimization?
authors: Boning Li, Longbo Huang
abstract: Solving imperfect-information games at scale rests on counterfactual regret minimization with the regret matching$^{+}$ (RM$^{+}$) update, and a seemingly minor implementation choice accounts for much of its practical speed: alternating the two players' updates, so that the second player responds to the strategy the first player just produced. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.

title: On the Sampling of Certain Dirichlet and Prime Sums at Gram Points and their Viscosity
authors: Yochay Jerby
abstract: Consider the Dirichlet polynomial and its prime-indexed sub-sum \[ \begin{array}{ccc} E(t) := \sum_{k\le \left[ \sqrt{ \frac{t}{2π} } \right]} \frac{e^{it\log k}}{\sqrt{k}}, & ; & E_1(t) := \sum_{\substack{p\le \left[ \sqrt{\frac{t}{2π}} \right]\\ p\ {\rm prime}}} \frac{e^{it\log p}}{\sqrt p}. \end{array} \] In this work we investigate the statistical and arithmetic properties of the sets \[ \mathcal{C}_N := \left\{ E(g_n):1\le n\le N \right\}, \qquad \mathcal{P}_N := \left\{ E_1(g_n):1\le n\le N \right\}, \] obtained by sampling these sums at the Gram points \(g_n\) of the Hardy \(Z\)-function. We refer to \(\mathcal{C}_N\) and \(\mathcal{P}_N\) as the full and prime \(N\)-th Gram clouds, respectively. The motivation is that the approximate functional equation expresses both \(Z(g_n)\) and \(Z'(g_n)\) through different projections of the same oscillatory phase configuration, suggesting that the geometry of these sampled sums may retain information about the local behavior of nearby zeros. Numerically, we find that Gram-point sampling produces highly non-generic geometric structures: good and isolated bad Gram points occupy markedly different regions of the clouds, the prime cloud of isolated bad points splits into two anisotropic lobes, and the position along the principal direction of the folded prime cloud is strongly correlated with the viscosity of the Hardy $Z$-function \( μ(g_n)=\left|\frac{Z'(g_n)}{Z(g_n)}\right|, \) with smallest-viscosity points concentrating near distinguished extremal regions of the lobes.

title: Experimental review on global polarization and spin alignment in heavy-ion collisions
authors: Takafumi Niida
abstract: Polarization phenomena in heavy-ion collisions have attracted considerable interest since the first experimental observation of global spin polarization. Over the past few years, particle polarization has emerged as a rapidly growing field, with new measurements that have stimulated intense theoretical efforts to understand the puzzling experimental results. In these proceedings, we review recent experimental progress on hyperon global polarization, local polarization along the beam direction, and vector-meson spin alignment in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, and newly emerging measurements of spin-spin correlations. These measurements provide new insights into the vortical structure of the quark-gluon plasma and the spin dynamics during the system evolution.

title: Cayley graphs of abelian groups, circular colorings and discrete fundamental groups
authors: Kengo Enami, Takahiro Matsushita
abstract: For each integer $k \ge 2$, we prove that an abelian group $Γ$ satisfies $\exp(Γ) \in \{1,\dots,k\} \cup \{2,4,\dots,2k\}$ if and only if it admits no non-bipartite Cayley graph whose circular chromatic number is strictly less than $2 + \frac{2}{k-1}$. This refines the algebraic characterization by Krebs and Sankar of abelian groups that admit $3$-chromatic Cayley graphs.

title: Synergistic charging of a quantum battery via Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and non-Markovian noise
authors: Si-Yu Zhang, Meng-Long Song, Hai-Tao Dong, Xue-Ke Song, Liu Ye, Dong Wang
abstract: Protecting quantum batteries from environmental noise remains a challenge. Using exact Burshtein-Kubo equations, we study a two-spin quantum battery with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) coupling under indepen dent local longitudinal random telegraph noise (RTN). At a fixed effective noise scale, the DM-assisted slow switching protocol yields a superadditive transient ergotropy gain and near-maximal ergotropy during the initial charging stage, while the no-DM slow-switching control reaches comparable ergotropy only in a later revival. A finite superadditive region persists at fixed RTN amplitude, with protocol-dependent location and gain. In the Ising model, the enhancement is nonmonotonic in DM strength, with intermediate coupling giving near-optimal performance. Dressed-channel analysis associates this enhancement with changes in transition frequencies and longitudinal-noise matrix elements that reduce slow-RTN spectral weight. Superadditivity also persists in the tested anisotropic XY model.

title: A variation on local trilinear form
authors: Yiyang Wang
abstract: Let $F$ be a $p$-adic field and $M$ the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2^3(F)$ consisting of triples with equal determinants. For each unitary principal series $L$-packet of $M$ whose central character is trivial on the diagonal $F^\times$, we determine its unique member distinguished by the diagonal $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$.

title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
authors: Antoine Bergerault, Cyrille Kone, Giorgia Ramponi
abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
authors: Sabine Häussler, Meritxell Cabrejo-Ponce, Ana Maria Torres, Baghdasar Baghdasaryan, Karen Lozano-Mendéz, Fabian Steinlechner
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
authors: Mohammad Pedramfar, Siamak Ravanbakhsh
abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

title: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
authors: Li Ma, Yan Zhuang, Jiawen Deng, Fuji Ren
abstract: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.

title: Low-Scale See-Saw Mechanism and the Majorana Nature of Heavy Neutrinos
authors: Takuya Okawa, S. T. Petcov
abstract: We investigate the possibility to determine the Majorana nature of the heavy Majorana neutrinos present in the low-scale type I seesaw mechanism of neutrino mass generation in experiments at $e^+ \text{-} e^-$ and $μ^+ \text{-} μ^-$ colliders. This is done on the examples of two specific symmetry-protected seesaw scenarios with two right-handed (RH) singlet neutrinos and one seesaw realization with three RH neutrinos. We use the forward-backward symmetry in the angular distribution of the heavy neutral leptons produced in the $e^+ \text{-} e^-$ and $μ^+ \text{-} μ^-$ collisions as an indicator of their Majorana nature. Our results indicate that the experiments at FCCee during its first phase of operation have a remarkable potential not only to discover the heavy neutral leptons associated with the type I seesaw mechanism if they have masses smaller than the $Z^0$-boson mass, but also to probe and provide evidence for their Majorana nature.

title: Scalar curvature, volume, and Weil-Petersson translation length
authors: Cameron Gates Rudd
abstract: We construct metrics on pseudoAnosov mapping tori that make every fiber an intrinsically hyperbolic stable minimal surface, and which have scalar curvature identically -6. Using this, we give a new proof (with improved constant) of an inequality bounding the hyperbolic volume of a pseudoAnosov mapping torus by the Weil-Petersson translation length (and consequently, the entropy) of its monodromy.

title: One generation of the Standard Model as a quantum error-correcting code
authors: Shiroman Prakash, K. L. Ramya
abstract: Together with a right-handed neutrino, the fermions of one generation of the Standard Model are labelled by five bits, a combinatorial structure tied to anomaly cancellation. We make this precise. Anomaly cancellation is the vanishing of a cubic form, the defining property of triorthogonal codes, the quantum error-correcting codes behind magic state distillation. Removing the right-handed neutrino gives a $[[15,1,3]]_p$ code for every prime $p$, including the Bravyi-Kitaev code for $p = 2$. For qutrits it is the unique shortest distance-three triorthogonal code.

title: High-frequency water megamasers as precision probes of black holes, galaxies and cosmology: A case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer
authors: Ingyin Zaw, C. M. Violette Impellizzeri, Dominic W. Pesce, Elizabeth Humphreys, Hannah R. Stacey, Sophie Venselaar, Chengyu Kuo, Jack Gallimore, Yoshiaki Hagiwara, Satoki Matsushita, Jim Braatz
abstract: Water megamasers in the circumnuclear disks of active galactic nuclei are among the most precise probes of supermassive black holes. VLBI imaging of 22 GHz disk masers has provided geometric distances to independently constrain $H_0$, accurate black hole mass measurements, and sub-parsec views of accretion disk geometry. ALMA has opened a new window into water maser transitions in the sub-mm/mm regime, which trace temperatures, densities and disk regions that are inaccessible at 22 GHz, and can be observed at higher spatial resolution and with less free-free absorption. However, current detections are limited to a few bright extragalactic masers in nearby galaxies. We present the case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer - ALMA2040 - that would open a new parameter space for maser studies. We show that a 10-fold increase in line sensitivity and three times longer baselines compared to ALMA would transform sub-mm maser studies from a few bright detections into a population-level probe, delivering black hole masses and geometric distances from sub-mm masers alone, independent of and complementary to 22 GHz measurements. Integrated into a VLBI array, ALMA2040 would resolve maser disks out to $>$160 Mpc, extend maser black hole masses into the largely untested intermediate-mass regime, reveal magnetic field structure in accretion disks through polarization studies, and test systematics in $H_0$ measurements.

title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
authors: Bowen Yang, Kaiming Jin, Zichen Ding, Zhenyu Wu, Zehao Li, Zhoumianze Liu, Kanzhi Cheng, Fangzhi Xu, Yanan Sun, Qiushi Sun, Yu Qiao
abstract: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step balanced optimization, while demonstrating cross-platform transfer on WindowsAgentArena. Our project homepage is at https://os-copilot.github.io/OS-Helix/.

title: ALMA2040: Submillimeter-wave Limb Sounding of Venus and Mars
authors: Hideo Sagawa, Arianna Piccialli, Miriam Rengel, Shohei Aoki, Thibault Cavalié, Alessandra Migliorini, Raphael Moreno, Arielle Moullet
abstract: Venus and Mars are unique laboratories for understanding the evolution and diversity of terrestrial planets. Despite their broadly similar rocky compositions, their atmospheres, climates, and surface environments have evolved into dramatically different states. Understanding the physical and chemical processes responsible for these divergent pathways is essential for interpreting terrestrial exoplanets and their habitability. By the 2040s, spacecraft missions will provide unprecedented close-up observations of Venus and Mars, while ground-based facilities can provide the long-term monitoring needed to place these snapshots in the context of atmospheric variability and planetary-scale circulation. ALMA2040 can uniquely bridge these two approaches by combining high-resolution submillimeter heterodyne spectroscopy with routinely accessible, extremely high angular resolution. In particular, high-resolution limb sounding would enable vertically resolved measurements of atmospheric winds, temperature, and trace species from the ground. An angular resolution of approximately 0.01" would allow spatial scales comparable to the atmospheric scale heights of Venus (around 5 km) and Mars (around 11 km) to be resolved. This capability would enable three-dimensional studies of Venusian upper-atmospheric circulation and Martian global dust storms, as well as systematic investigations of CO2 photochemistry, water loss through HDO/H2O fractionation, and Venusian sulfur chemistry and cloud formation. By repeatedly observing different local times, seasons, and solar-activity conditions, ALMA2040 would extend spacecraft measurements from snapshots to long-term four-dimensional characterization. It would therefore provide a unique observational framework for directly connecting spacecraft discoveries with the temporal and spatial evolution of planetary atmospheres.

title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Arshad Rahman, Adnan Aziz, Ajith Prabhudev, Amin Farmahini, Ben Rhoads, Benson Ma, Brian Shi, Cen Zhao, CK Luk, Dingming Wu, Emad El-Haraty, Eric Chen, Frank Li, Gary Huang, Gefei Zuo, Haoran Zhang, Hiwot Kassa, Hongyi Zeng, Jack Taylor, Jeremy Hadidjojo, John Donati, Jonathan Sheffield, Julio Machado Silva, Karthik Ganesan, Kent Russell, KR Kishore, Lei Tian, Liu Ke, Muhammad Osama, Peng Chen, Rakesh Hemnani, Ryan Swann, Saleel Kudchadker, Shankar Yanamandram, Shobhit Kanaujia, Shucai Xiao, Srinath Bayareddy, Srinivas Vaidyanathan, Sudharssun Subramanian, Supadchaya Puangpontip, Taylor Robie, Tianhao Huang, Tyler Hart, Viswesh Sankaran, Weijun Jiang, Wenkai Du, Xiaodong Wang, Xiaohu Guo, Yao Rong, Yinbin Ma, Yue Dong, Yuzhen Huang, Yvonne Liu, Zhan Shu, Dan Rabinovitsj, Ajit Mathews, Chunqiang Tang
abstract: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.

title: Stability Analysis in IBR-Dominated Grids: Model-Based and Data-Driven Methodologies
authors: Federico Cecati, Yang Wu, Florian Dörfler, Marco Liserre, Xiongfei Wang, Elisabetta Tedeschi
abstract: Stability issues in converter-dominated grids have a multifold nature, where static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena can influence each other. Capturing the interplay among these different stability aspects requires a rethinking of conventional modeling and analysis tools for power systems. As a further complication, Intellectual Property protection among manufacturers and system operators makes detailed converters and grid models unattainable. This motivates the use of data-driven approaches for stability analysis and control, nevertheless achieving an insightful representation of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena from data still leaves many open questions. This paper discusses model-based and data-driven methodologies for stability analysis of converter-dominated grids. The instability mechanisms of static, small-signal and large-signal phenomena are conceptually explained, and the capability of different modeling and analysis tools to investigate them is examined. The effectiveness of data-driven methodologies to analyze instability phenomena in their multifold nature is debated, and the challenges on data completeness, model generalization under untrained conditions, physical interpretability, and uncertainty awareness are discussed.

title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
authors: Weyner Ccuiro, Rosario Fazio, Alessandro Silva
abstract: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with Néel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates $γ_{\pm}$ describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation ($γ_+ > γ_-$) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

title: FutureLift: Lifting Trajectory Proposals into Bidirectional Future Graphs for Motion Forecasting
authors: Daniel Grimm, J. Marius Zöllner
abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.

title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory
authors: Sebastian-Antonio Toma, Jean de Kernier, Mike Ply, Oliviu Matei
abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.

title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
authors: Manish Chaudhary, Tim Byrnes
abstract: We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

title: Dark Matter in the Galaxy: Insights from the Dynamics of Stellar Streams
authors: Mohammad Ayaz, Priya Hasan
abstract: Dark matter constitutes most of the matter in the Universe, yet its fundamental nature and distribution remain poorly understood. Stellar streams, formed through the tidal disruption of globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, provide powerful tracers of the Milky Way's gravitational potential and dark matter halo. In this review, we examine how stellar stream morphology and kinematics can constrain the halo's structure, shape, and substructure. We discuss key observational signatures, including stream gaps, spurs, and perturbations, and investigate five prominent streams: Sagittarius, GD-1, Palomar 5, Orphan-Chenab, and Cetus Polar. We summarize analytical, statistical, and Bayesian methods used to model stellar streams and infer dark matter properties, highlighting challenges arising from parameter degeneracies, incomplete observations, progenitor uncertainties, and time-dependent perturbations, particularly those associated with the Large Magellanic Cloud. Finally, we discuss how upcoming astrometric and photometric surveys, together with improved dynamical modelling, may strengthen constraints on the Milky Way's dark matter distribution and help distinguish between cold, warm, and self-interacting dark matter scenarios.

title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing
authors: Tianxiang Fei, Jiazheng Kang, Mao Zheng, Xingyan He, Xiang Yu
abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.

title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
authors: Bingxiang He, Pengqi Sun, Shihao Peng, Shaoxuan Li, Huiyu Xiao, Hongjian Shi, Zixuan Fu, Ziqing Qiao, Yuxin Zuo, Cheng Qian, Xinqiang Yu, Jiayi Li, Xiusi Chen, Yizhen Song, Xiangyang Wang, Iofai Lei, Yudong Wang, Ning Ding, Zhiyuan Liu, Xiaozhi Wang, Chaojun Xiao
